# `ghlike` — behavioral spec

`ghlike` is a forge client in the gh mold: a deep command tree (`noun verb`,
down to `noun noun verb`) where every listing command serves humans by
default and machines through `--json` with **field selection**. It reads one
frozen, built-in forge state; there are no mutating commands.

## The frozen forge state

Repositories:

| name | description | visibility |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `demo/alpha` | Alpha service | public |
| `demo/beta` | Beta tools | private |

Pull requests (all in `demo/alpha`), in number order:

| number | title | state | author | draft |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Add pager | open | alice | false |
| 2 | Fix theme | merged | bob | false |
| 3 | Docs pass | open | alice | true |

Checks: PR 1 has `build` = pass and `lint` = fail (in that order); PR 2 has
`build` = pass and `lint` = pass; PR 3 has no checks.

## The command tree

```text
ghlike
├── auth status
├── repo view <owner/name>
└── pr
    ├── list
    ├── view <number>
    └── checks
        └── list <number>
```

Invoking a group (`ghlike pr`, `ghlike pr checks`) without a subcommand is a
usage error: exit 2, guidance on stderr, nothing on stdout. `--help` works at
every level and exits 0 with help on stdout.

Tables follow one layout rule: columns separated by a single space, each
column but the last padded to its widest rendered cell (header included when
shown).

### `ghlike auth status`

```text
Logged in as corpus-bot
```

### `ghlike repo view <owner/name>`

```text
demo/alpha
Alpha service
visibility: public
```

Unknown repository: exit 1, empty stdout, and on stderr:

```text
ghlike: repository not found: <owner/name>
```

### `ghlike pr list`

```text
NUMBER TITLE     STATE
1      Add pager open
2      Fix theme merged
3      Docs pass open
```

### `ghlike pr view <number>`

```text
#2 Fix theme
state: merged
author: bob
```

Unknown number: exit 1, empty stdout, stderr
`ghlike: no pull request found: <number>`.

### `ghlike pr checks list <number>`

Headerless rows, `<name> <status>`, same padding rule:

```text
build pass
lint  fail
```

## `--json <fields>` — machine output with field selection

`pr list`, `pr view`, and `pr checks list` accept `--json` with a
comma-separated field list. Available fields: `number`, `title`, `state`,
`author`, `draft` for pull requests; `name`, `status` for checks.

- Output is pure JSON on stdout: `pr list` and `checks list` emit an array
  of objects, `pr view` a single object, each object carrying exactly the
  requested fields. `number` is a JSON number, `draft` a JSON boolean,
  everything else strings.
- JSON output is byte-boring by design: never styled, never paged, never
  framed with human prose — even on an attended color-capable terminal.
- An unknown field is an error: exit 1, empty stdout, and a stderr message
  naming the rejected field and listing the valid ones.

## Exit codes

| code | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | success |
| 1 | domain errors: unknown repo, unknown PR, unknown `--json` field |
| 2 | usage errors: group without subcommand, unknown subcommand or flag |

content.content:
1	# Standout
2	
3	**Test your data. Render your view.**
4	
5	Standout is a CLI framework for Rust that enforces separation between logic and
6	presentation. Keep application behavior in a CLI-free library; handlers adapt
7	that behavior into serializable CLI view data instead of strings.
8	
9	## The Problem
10	
11	CLI code that mixes logic with `println!` statements is impossible to unit test:
12	
13	```rust
14	// You can't unit test this—it writes directly to stdout
15	fn list_command(show_all: bool) {
16	    let todos = storage::list().unwrap();
17	    println!("Your Todos:");
18	    for todo in todos.iter() {
19	        if show_all || todo.status == Status::Pending {
20	            println!("  {} {}", if todo.done { "[x]" } else { "[ ]" }, todo.title);
21	        }
22	    }
23	}
24	```
25	
26	The only way to test this is regex on captured stdout. That's fragile, verbose, and couples your tests to presentation details.
27	
28	## The Solution
29	
30	With Standout, the library owns behavior, handlers return CLI view data, and
31	the framework handles rendering:
32	
33	```rust
34	#[handler]
35	fn list(
36	    #[flag] all: bool,
37	    #[ctx] ctx: &CommandContext,
38	) -> Result<Output<TodoListView>, anyhow::Error> {
39	    let store = ctx.app_state.get_required::<TodoStore>()?;
40	    let filter = if all { TodoFilter::All } else { TodoFilter::Pending };
41	    let todos = store.list(filter).into_iter().map(TodoView::from).collect();
42	    let total = todos.len();
43	    Ok(Output::Render(TodoListView { todos, total }))
44	}
45	
46	#[test]
47	fn test_list_returns_pending_view() {
48	    let Output::Render(result) = list(false, &ctx).unwrap() else {
49	        panic!("expected rendered data");
50	    };
51	    assert!(result.todos.iter().all(|todo| !todo.done));
52	}
53	```
54	
55	Test filtering and state transitions through the library interface. Test only
56	the mapping and returned view struct in the handler. No stdout capture, regex,
57	or template coupling. See the
58	[production-shaped application](guides/production-shaped-example.md).
59	
60	## Standing Out
61	
62	What Standout provides:
63	
64	- Enforced architecture splitting data and presentation
65	- Logic is testable as any Rust code — and full CLI invocations are testable in-process via the [`standout-test`](guides/intro-to-testing.md) harness, without subprocess spawning or stdout parsing
66	- Boilerplateless: declaratively link your handlers to command names and templates, Standout handles the rest
67	- Autodispatch: save keystrokes with auto dispatch from the known command tree
68	- Free [output handling](topics/output-modes.md): rich terminal with graceful degradation, plus structured data (JSON, YAML, CSV)
69	- Finely crafted output:
70	  - File-based [templates](crates/render/topics/templating.md) for content and CSS for styling
71	  - Rich styling with [adaptive properties](crates/render/topics/styling-system.md) (light/dark modes), inheritance, and full theming
72	  - Powerful templating through [MiniJinja](https://github.com/mitsuhiko/minijinja), including partials (reusable, smaller templates for models displayed in multiple places)
73	  - [Hot reload](crates/render/topics/file-system-resources.md): changes to templates and styles don't require compiling
74	  - Declarative layout support for [tabular data](crates/render/guides/intro-to-tabular.md)
75	
76	## Quick Start
77	
78	### 1. Define Your Commands and Handlers
79	
80	Use the `Dispatch` derive macro to connect commands to typed handler adapters.
81	
82	```rust
83	use standout::cli::{CommandContext, Dispatch, Output};
84	use standout::handler;
85	use clap::{Parser, Subcommand};
86	use serde::Serialize;
87	use todo_core::{Todo, TodoFilter, TodoStore};
88	
89	#[derive(Parser)]
90	#[command(name = "myapp")]
91	pub struct Cli {
92	    #[command(subcommand)]
93	    pub command: Commands,
94	}
95	
96	#[derive(Subcommand, Dispatch)]
97	#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]  // handlers are in the `handlers` module
98	pub enum Commands {
99	    #[dispatch(pure)]
100	    List,
101	    #[dispatch(pure)]
102	    Add { title: String },
103	}
104	
105	#[derive(Serialize)]
106	struct TodoResult {
107	    todos: Vec<Todo>,
108	}
109	
110	mod handlers {
111	    use super::*;
112	
113	    #[handler]
114	    pub fn list(#[ctx] ctx: &CommandContext) -> Result<Output<TodoResult>, anyhow::Error> {
115	        let core = ctx.app_state.get_required::<TodoStore>()?;
116	        Ok(Output::Render(TodoResult { todos: core.list(TodoFilter::Pending) }))
117	    }
118	
119	    #[handler]
120	    pub fn add(
121	        #[arg] title: String,
122	        #[ctx] ctx: &CommandContext,
123	    ) -> Result<Output<TodoResult>, anyhow::Error> {
124	        let core = ctx.app_state.get_required::<TodoStore>()?;
125	        Ok(Output::Render(TodoResult { todos: vec![core.add(title)?] }))
126	    }
127	}
128	```
129	
130	### 2. Define Your Presentation
131	
132	Templates use MiniJinja with semantic style tags. Styles are defined separately in CSS.
133	
134	```jinja
135	{# list.jinja #}
136	[title]My Todos[/title]
137	{% for todo in todos %}
138	  - {{ todo.title }} ([status]{{ todo.status }}[/status])
139	{% endfor %}
140	```
141	
142	```css
143	/* styles/default.css */
144	.title { color: cyan; font-weight: bold; }
145	.status { color: yellow; }
146	```
147	
148	### 3. Wire It Up
149	
150	```rust
151	use clap::CommandFactory;
152	use standout::cli::App;
153	use standout::{embed_templates, embed_styles};
154	use todo_core::TodoStore;
155	
156	fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
157	    let store = TodoStore::load("todos.json")?;
158	    let app = App::builder()
159	        .app_state(store) // the handlers above read it back with `get_required`
160	        .templates(embed_templates!("src/templates"))
161	        .styles(embed_styles!("src/styles"))
162	        .default_theme("default")
163	        .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())? // Register handlers from derive macro
164	        .build()?;
165	
166	    app.run(Cli::command(), std::env::args());
167	    Ok(())
168	}
169	```
170	
171	Run it:
172	
173	```bash
174	myapp list              # Rich terminal output with colors
175	myapp list --output json    # JSON for scripting
176	myapp list --output yaml    # YAML for config files
177	myapp list --output text    # Plain text, no ANSI codes
178	```
179	
180	## Features
181	
182	### Architecture
183	
184	- CLI-free library separated from shell presentation
185	- Handlers adapt library results; framework handles rendering
186	- Core behavior and CLI adapters testable without stdout capture
187	
188	### Output Modes
189	
190	- Rich terminal output with colors and styles
191	- Automatic JSON, YAML, CSV serialization from the same handler
192	- Graceful degradation when terminal lacks capabilities
193	
194	### Rendering
195	
196	- [MiniJinja](https://github.com/mitsuhiko/minijinja) templates with semantic style tags
197	- CSS stylesheets with light/dark mode support
198	- Hot reload during development—edit templates without recompiling
199	- Tabular layouts with alignment, truncation, and Unicode support
200	
201	### Integration
202	
203	- Clap integration with automatic dispatch
204	- Declarative command registration via derive macros
205	
206	## Installation
207	
208	```bash
209	cargo add standout standout-dispatch
210	```
211	
212	## Migrating an Existing CLI
213	
214	Already have a CLI? Standout supports incremental adoption. `run` reports
215	whether Standout handled the command:
216	
217	```rust
218	if !app.run(Cli::command(), std::env::args()) {
219	    your_existing_dispatch();
220	}
221	```
222	
223	Use `run_to_string(...)` and match `DispatchResult::NoMatch(matches)` on
224	`into_outcome()` when the legacy dispatcher needs the unmatched `ArgMatches`.
225	
226	See the [Partial Adoption Guide](crates/dispatch/topics/partial-adoption.md) for the full migration path.
227

231	- **[Introduction to Testing](guides/intro-to-testing.md)** — Why Standout CLIs are testable by design, and how the `standout-test` harness replaces slow, brittle subprocess tests with fast in-process ones.
232	- [Introduction to Rendering](crates/render/guides/intro-to-rendering.md) — Creating polished terminal output
233	- [Introduction to Tabular](crates/render/guides/intro-to-tabular.md) — Building aligned, readable tabular layouts
234	- [All Topics](topics/index.md) — In-depth documentation for specific systems

1	# Fast Paced intro to your First Standout Based Command
2	
3	This is a terse and direct how to for more experienced developers or at least the ones in a hurry.
4	It skimps rationale, design and other useful bits you can read from the [longer form version](intro-to-standout.md)
5	
6	## Prerequisites
7	
8	A cli app, that uses clap for arg parsing.
9	A CLI-free library function that owns the application behavior, plus a handler
10	that adapts parsed CLI input to that library and returns serializable view data.
11	The library must not depend on Clap, Standout, `CommandContext`, templates,
12	styles, environment lookup, or app construction.
13	
14	For this guide's purpose we'll use a fictitious "list" command of our todo list manager
15	
16	## The core and its handler adapter
17	
18	The library owns filtering, validation, and state transitions. The handler is a
19	CLI adapter: it receives parsed arguments, calls the library, and returns a
20	serializable CLI view:
21	
22	```rust
23	    #[handler]
24	    pub fn list(
25	        #[flag] all: bool,
26	        #[ctx] ctx: &CommandContext,
27	    ) -> Result<Output<TodoResult>, anyhow::Error> {
28	        let store = ctx.app_state.get_required::<TodoStore>()?;
29	        let filter = if all { TodoFilter::All } else { TodoFilter::Pending };
30	        Ok(Output::Render(TodoResult::from(store.list(filter))))
31	    }
32	```
33	
34	## Making it outstanding
35	
36	### 1. The File System
37	
38	Create a templates/list.jinja and styles/default.css:
39	
40	```text
41	    src/
42	        ├── handlers.rs         # where list it
43	        ├── templates/          # standout will match templates name against rel. paths from temp root, here
44	            ├── list.jinja      # the template to render list, name matched against the command name
45	        ├── styles/             #  likewise for themes, this sets a theme called "default"
46	            ├── default.css     # the default style for the command, filename will be the theme name
47	```
48	
49	### 2. Define your styles
50	
51	```css
52	    .done {
53	        text-decoration: line-through;
54	        color: gray;
55	    }
56	    .pending {
57	        font-weight: bold;
58	        color: white;
59	    }
60	    .index {
61	        color: yellow;
62	    }
63	```
64	
65	### 3. Write your template
66	
67	```Jinja
68	    {% if message %}
69	        [message]{{ message }} [/message]
70	    {% endif %}
71	    {% for todo in todos %}
72	        [index]{{ loop.index }}.[/index] [{{ todo.status }}]{{ todo.title }}[/{{ todo.status }}]
73	    {% endfor %}
74	```
75	
76	### 4. Putting it all together
77	
78	Configure the app:
79	
80	```rust
81	    let app = App::builder()
82	        .app_state(Database::connect()?)                 // Optional: shared state for handlers
83	        .templates(embed_templates!("src/templates"))    // Sets the root template path
84	        .styles(embed_styles!("src/styles"))             // Likewise the styles root
85	        .default_theme("default")                        // Use styles/default.css
86	        .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())?          // Register handlers from derive macro
87	        .build()?;
88	```
89	
90	> Handlers access shared state via `ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?`. See [App State and Extensions](../crates/dispatch/topics/app-state.md) for details.
91	
92	Connect your logic to a command name and template. The variant declares every
93	argument its handler asks for — `list` takes `#[flag] all`, so `List` carries
94	an `all` field for it to read:
95	
96	```rust
97	    #[derive(Subcommand, Dispatch)]
98	    #[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
99	    pub enum Commands {
100	          // ...
101	          #[dispatch(pure)]
102	          List {
103	              #[arg(long)]
104	              all: bool,
105	          },
106	    }
107	```
108	
109	And finally, run in main, the autodispatcher:
110	
111	```rust
112	    if !app.run(Cli::command(), std::env::args()) {
113	        // If some commands still use manual dispatch, fall back here.
114	        legacy_dispatch();
115	    }
116	```
117	
118	When the fallback needs the unmatched `ArgMatches`, call `run_with(cmd, args,
119	target, sources)` instead of `run`, and match `DispatchResult::NoMatch(matches)`
120	on the result's `into_outcome()`.
121

1	# The `#[dispatch(…)]` and `#[handler]` Reference
2	
3	Two macros carry the blessed idiom. `#[derive(Dispatch)]` on an enum binds
4	command names to handler functions; `#[handler]` on a function turns it into
5	something the dispatcher can call. This page is the complete list of what each
6	one accepts.
7	
8	Both name mappings on this page — a variant name to a command name, and a
9	parameter name to a clap argument id — are contract, because they decide the
10	words a user types in a shell script. See
11	[What Is Contract](stability.md#4-the-two-name-mappings-a-user-types-on-the-command-line).
12	
13	## `#[derive(Dispatch)]`
14	
15	### The container attribute
16	
17	One attribute goes on the enum, and it is required:
18	
19	```rust,ignore
20	#[derive(Dispatch)]
21	#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
22	enum Commands { /* … */ }
23	```
24	
25	`handlers = <module path>` names the module the derive looks each variant's
26	handler up in. Without it, expansion fails with `missing #[dispatch(handlers =
27	path)] attribute`.
28	
29	### From a variant name to a command name
30	
31	A variant registers under its **kebab-case** name — `ListUnits` becomes
32	`list-units` — which is the spelling clap's own derive gives the subcommand.
33	`#[dispatch(name = "…")]` renames one variant.
34	
35	A `name` may not be empty and may not contain `.`: dispatch splits registration
36	paths on `.`, so such a name would register a nested path no clap subcommand
37	declares. Nesting is `#[dispatch(nested)]`, below.
38	
39	A registered path that no clap subcommand can reach is a loud error naming the
40	path, raised by `App::run` and `App::verify_command` before dispatch.
41	
42	### From a variant name to a handler function
43	
44	The handler is looked up under the variant's **snake_case** name in the
45	`handlers` module — `ListUnits` calls `handlers::list_units`. Two attributes
46	change that:
47	
48	- `#[dispatch(pure)]` appends `__handler`, so the derive calls
49	  `handlers::list_units__handler` — the wrapper `#[handler]` generated. Use it
50	  whenever the handler function carries `#[handler]`, which is the blessed
51	  style. The derive registers through a closure taking `HandlerResult<T>`, so a
52	  `pure` handler must be annotated `-> Result<Output<T>, E>` or
53	  `-> Result<(), E>`; a plain `-> Result<T, E>` fails expansion. See
54	  [what `#[handler]` generates](#what-handler-generates).
55	- `#[dispatch(handler = <path>)]` names the function outright and ignores the
56	  inferred name.
57	
58	The two are mutually exclusive, and expansion rejects the pair with a message
59	naming both. Without `pure`, the derive calls the named function directly, so
60	that function must already have the dispatch signature.
61	
62	### Every variant attribute
63	
64	Several `#[dispatch(…)]` attributes may sit on one variant; they merge before
65	anything reads them.
66	
67	| Attribute | Form | What it does |
68	| --- | --- | --- |
69	| `name` | `name = "…"` | Registers the command under this name instead of the variant's kebab-case name. Not empty, no `.`. |
70	| `handler` | `handler = <path>` | Calls this function instead of the inferred one. Excludes `pure`. |
71	| `pure` | flag | The handler carries `#[handler]`: append `__handler` to the inferred name. Excludes `handler` and `simple`. |
72	| `simple` | flag | The handler takes only `&ArgMatches`, with no `&CommandContext`. Excludes `pure`. |
73	| `nested` | flag | The variant is a subcommand group. Requires a single-field tuple variant wrapping another `Dispatch` enum. |
74	| `skip` | flag | Registers nothing for this variant. |
75	| `default` | flag | Runs this command on a naked invocation. At most one variant per enum. |
76	| `template_name` | `template_name = "…"` | Names the template registry entry instead of using the convention. Excludes `silent`, `binary` and `structured_only`. |
77	| `silent` | flag | The command renders nothing. Excludes `binary`, `structured_only`, `template_name`. |
78	| `binary` | flag | The command writes bytes rather than a rendered page. Same exclusions. |
79	| `structured_only` | flag | The command has output only in the structured modes. Same exclusions. |
80	| `list_view` | flag | Renders through the framework's built-in `standout/list-view` template, unless `template_name` also appears, and attaches a tabular spec to the handler's `Output::Render`. |
81	| `item_type` | `item_type = "…"` | Names the `Tabular`-implementing item type `list_view` builds its spec from. |
82	| `questionnaire` | `questionnaire = <path>` | Resolves this questionnaire type before the handler runs. |
83	| `pre_dispatch` | `pre_dispatch = <path>` | Runs this hook before the handler. |
84	| `post_dispatch` | `post_dispatch = <path>` | Runs this hook after the handler, before rendering. |
85	| `post_output` | `post_output = <path>` | Runs this hook after the output is produced. |
86	| `pipe_to` | `pipe_to = "…"` | Sends the output to this command and keeps the original. |
87	| `pipe_through` | `pipe_through = "…"` | Replaces the output with this command's stdout. |
88	| `pipe_to_clipboard` | flag | Sends the output to the clipboard. |
89	
90	An unrecognized key fails expansion with a message listing every key above.
91	
92	### Nested commands
93	
94	`#[dispatch(nested)]` marks a variant that wraps another `Dispatch` enum:
95	
96	```rust,ignore
97	#[derive(Dispatch)]
98	#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
99	enum Commands {
100	    #[dispatch(nested)]
101	    Pr(PrCommands),
102	}
103	```
104	
105	The derive registers the group rather than a command, and the inner enum's own
106	variants register beneath it. Registration paths are dot-joined as the
107	recursion descends, so `pr checks list` registers the path `pr.checks.list`.
108	
109	### How a command finds its template
110	
111	With no `template_name` and no absence marker (`silent`, `binary`,
112	`structured_only`), the template name **is** the registration path with each
113	`.` replaced by `/`, and **no extension appended**:
114	
115	| Registration path | Template name |
116	| --- | --- |
117	| `list` | `list` |
118	| `pr.checks.list` | `pr/checks/list` |
119	
120	The registry then resolves that name against `.jinja`, `.jinja2`, `.j2`,
121	`.stpl` and `.txt`, in that priority order — so a nested `pr checks list`
122	command is rendered by `src/templates/pr/checks/list.jinja`. A name may be
123	looked up with or without an extension; the extension is stripped and the base
124	name retried.
125	
126	`#[dispatch(template_name = "…")]` replaces that name with a registry entry you
127	choose, which is how two commands share one template.
128	
129	## `#[handler]`
130	
131	### Parameter attributes
132	
133	Every typed parameter carries one of four attributes, references included: the
134	macro reads the value out of `ArgMatches` (or hands over the dispatcher's own
135	reference) by the attribute, never by the type, so a `&CommandContext` still
136	needs `#[ctx]` and an `&ArgMatches` still needs `#[matches]`.
137	
138	| Attribute | Type | Where the value comes from |
139	| --- | --- | --- |
140	| `#[flag]` | `bool` | `matches.get_flag(id)` |
141	| `#[arg]` | `T` | a required argument |
142	| `#[arg]` | `Option<T>` | an optional argument |
143	| `#[arg]` | `Vec<T>` | a repeated argument |
144	| `#[ctx]` | `&CommandContext` | the dispatcher |
145	| `#[matches]` | `&ArgMatches` | the dispatcher, unparsed |
146	
147	### From a parameter name to a clap argument id
148	
149	**Underscores become hyphens.** A parameter named `no_legend` reads the
150	argument whose id is `no-legend`.
151	
152	Clap's own derive ids an argument by the field name it comes from, so the two
153	disagree unless one of them says so. Either side can:
154	
155	```rust,ignore
156	#[arg(id = "no-legend")]        // on the clap-derive field
157	no_legend: bool,
158	
159	#[flag(name = "no_legend")]     // on the handler parameter
160	no_legend: bool,
161	```
162	
163	`app.verify_command(&cmd)` reports the mismatch at build time rather than
164	leaving it to a runtime `get_flag` panic.
165	
166	A parameter named with a raw identifier drops the `r#` first, the way clap's
167	derive drops it from a field name: `r#type` reads the argument id `type`.
168	
169	### What `#[handler]` generates
170	
171	For `fn list`, four items:
172	
173	| Item | What it is |
174	| --- | --- |
175	| `list` | the original function, unchanged apart from the parameter attributes being removed — still directly callable from a test |
176	| `list__handler(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext)` | the wrapper that extracts the arguments and calls `list`. It returns **the function's own annotated return type**, verbatim |
177	| `list__expected_args() -> Vec<ExpectedArg>` | what `verify_command` reads |
178	| `list_Handler` | a unit struct implementing `Handler` — the registrable item |
179	
180	The `Result<T, E>` to `Output::Render` wrap happens inside `Handler::handle`,
181	not inside `list__handler`, and that is what makes the two registration methods
182	accept different things. `AppBuilder::command_with` takes an `impl Handler`, so
183	`handlers::list_Handler` works for any of the three return shapes.
184	`GroupBuilder::command_with` — which is what `#[derive(Dispatch)]` reaches —
185	takes a closure returning `HandlerResult<T>`, so it accepts
186	`handlers::list__handler` only when the function was annotated
187	`-> Result<Output<T>, E>` or `-> Result<(), E>`. The un-suffixed
188	`handlers::list` is registrable through neither.
189	
190	See the [handler contract](../crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md) for
191	the return types themselves.
192	
193	## A worked example
194	
195	Every attribute below is exercised by
196	`crates/standout-fixtures/src/derive_surface.rs`, which compiles under
197	`deny(warnings)` against a single `standout` dependency.
198	
199	```rust
200	use clap::{Arg, ArgAction, ArgMatches, Command};
201	use standout::cli::{App, CommandContext, Dispatch, Output};
202	use standout::{handler, EmbeddedTemplates};
203	
204	#[derive(serde::Serialize)]
205	pub struct Units {
206	    pub names: Vec<String>,
207	}
208	
209	pub mod handlers {
210	    use super::*;
211	
212	    #[handler]
213	    pub fn list_units(#[flag] all: bool) -> Result<Output<Units>, anyhow::Error> {
214	        let mut names = vec!["ssh".to_string()];
215	        if all {
216	            names.push("cron".to_string());
217	        }
218	        Ok(Output::Render(Units { names }))
219	    }
220	
221	    #[handler]
222	    pub fn about(#[ctx] _ctx: &CommandContext) -> Result<Output<Units>, anyhow::Error> {
223	        Ok(Output::Render(Units { names: vec!["unitctl".to_string()] }))
224	    }
225	
226	    #[handler]
227	    pub fn reload(#[matches] _matches: &ArgMatches) -> Result<(), anyhow::Error> {
228	        Ok(())
229	    }
230	}
231	
232	#[derive(Dispatch)]
233	#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
234	pub enum Commands {
235	    #[dispatch(pure, default)]
236	    ListUnits,
237	    #[dispatch(pure, name = "about-this")]
238	    About,
239	    #[dispatch(pure, silent)]
240	    Reload,
241	}
242	
243	const TEMPLATES: &[(&str, &str)] = &[
244	    ("list-units", "{{ names | join(', ') }}"),
245	    ("about-this", "{{ names | join(', ') }}"),
246	];
247	
248	/// The clap surface `Commands` is registered against. `Dispatch` connects a
249	/// variant to a handler; declaring the handler's arguments stays clap's job,
250	/// so `list-units` carries the `all` its handler reads.
251	fn command() -> Command {
252	    Command::new("unitctl")
253	        .subcommand(
254	            Command::new("list-units")
255	                .arg(Arg::new("all").long("all").action(ArgAction::SetTrue)),
256	        )
257	        .subcommand(Command::new("about-this"))
258	        .subcommand(Command::new("reload"))
259	}
260	
261	fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
262	    let app: App = App::builder()
263	        .templates(EmbeddedTemplates::new(TEMPLATES, ""))
264	        .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())?
265	        .build()?;
266	    app.verify_command(&command())?;
267	    Ok(())
268	}
269	```
270	
271	`ListUnits` registers the command `list-units`, calls
272	`handlers::list_units__handler`, renders the registry entry `list-units`, and
273	runs on a naked invocation. Its `#[flag] all` parameter reads the clap argument
274	`all` that `command()` declares on that subcommand; `verify_command` is what
275	reports the two drifting apart, instead of leaving it to a `get_flag` panic on
276	the first invocation. `About` registers `about-this` and renders the
277	entry of the same name, because `name` changes the registration path and the
278	convention follows it. `Reload` registers `reload`, calls
279	`handlers::reload__handler` and renders nothing, so it needs no template.
280

choose, which is how two commands share one template.

## `#[handler]`

### Parameter attributes

Every typed parameter carries one of four attributes, references included: the
macro reads the value out of `ArgMatches` (or hands over the dispatcher's own
reference) by the attribute, never by the type, so a `&CommandContext` still
needs `#[ctx]` and an `&ArgMatches` still needs `#[matches]`.

| Attribute | Type | Where the value comes from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `#[flag]` | `bool` | `matches.get_flag(id)` |
| `#[arg]` | `T` | a required argument |
| `#[arg]` | `Option<T>` | an optional argument |
| `#[arg]` | `Vec<T>` | a repeated argument |
| `#[ctx]` | `&CommandContext` | the dispatcher |
| `#[matches]` | `&ArgMatches` | the dispatcher, unparsed |

### From a parameter name to a clap argument id

**Underscores become hyphens.** A parameter named `no_legend` reads the
argument whose id is `no-legend`.

Clap's own derive ids an argument by the field name it comes from, so the two
disagree unless one of them says so. Either side can:

```rust,ignore
#[arg(id = "no-legend")]        // on the clap-derive field
no_legend: bool,

#[flag(name = "no_legend")]     // on the handler parameter
no_legend: bool,
```

`app.verify_command(&cmd)` reports the mismatch at build time rather than
leaving it to a runtime `get_flag` panic.

A parameter named with a raw identifier drops the `r#` first, the way clap's
derive drops it from a field name: `r#type` reads the argument id `type`.

### What `#[handler]` generates

For `fn list`, four items:

| Item | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `list` | the original function, unchanged apart from the parameter attributes being removed — still directly callable from a test |
| `list__handler(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext)` | the wrapper that extracts the arguments and calls `list`. It returns **the function's own annotated return type**, verbatim |
| `list__expected_args() -> Vec<ExpectedArg>` | what `verify_command` reads |
| `list_Handler` | a unit struct implementing `Handler` — the registrable item |

The `Result<T, E>` to `Output::Render` wrap happens inside `Handler::handle`,
not inside `list__handler`, and that is what makes the two registration methods
accept different things. `AppBuilder::command_with` takes an `impl Handler`, so
`handlers::list_Handler` works for any of the three return shapes.
`GroupBuilder::command_with` — which is what `#[derive(Dispatch)]` reaches —
takes a closure returning `HandlerResult<T>`, so it accepts
`handlers::list__handler` only when the function was annotated
`-> Result<Output<T>, E>` or `-> Result<(), E>`. The un-suffixed
`handlers::list` is registrable through neither.

See the [handler contract](../crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md) for
the return types themselves.

## A worked example

Every attribute below is exercised by
`crates/standout-fixtures/src/derive_surface.rs`, which compiles under
`deny(warnings)` against a single `standout` dependency.

```rust
use clap::{Arg, ArgAction, ArgMatches, Command};
use standout::cli::{App, CommandContext, Dispatch, Output};
use standout::{handler, EmbeddedTemplates};

#[derive(serde::Serialize)]
pub struct Units {
    pub names: Vec<String>,
}

pub mod handlers {
    use super::*;

    #[handler]
    pub fn list_units(#[flag] all: bool) -> Result<Output<Units>, anyhow::Error> {
        let mut names = vec!["ssh".to_string()];
        if all {
            names.push("cron".to_string());
        }
        Ok(Output::Render(Units { names }))
    }

    #[handler]
    pub fn about(#[ctx] _ctx: &CommandContext) -> Result<Output<Units>, anyhow::Error> {
        Ok(Output::Render(Units { names: vec!["unitctl".to_string()] }))
    }

    #[handler]
    pub fn reload(#[matches] _matches: &ArgMatches) -> Result<(), anyhow::Error> {
        Ok(())
    }
}

#[derive(Dispatch)]
#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
pub enum Commands {
    #[dispatch(pure, default)]
    ListUnits,
    #[dispatch(pure, name = "about-this")]
    About,
    #[dispatch(pure, silent)]
    Reload,
}

const TEMPLATES: &[(&str, &str)] = &[
    ("list-units", "{{ names | join(', ') }}"),
    ("about-this", "{{ names | join(', ') }}"),
];

/// The clap surface `Commands` is registered against. `Dispatch` connects a
/// variant to a handler; declaring the handler's arguments stays clap's job,
/// so `list-units` carries the `all` its handler reads.
fn command() -> Command {
    Command::new("unitctl")
        .subcommand(
            Command::new("list-units")
                .arg(Arg::new("all").long("all").action(ArgAction::SetTrue)),
        )
        .subcommand(Command::new("about-this"))
        .subcommand(Command::new("reload"))
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let app: App = App::builder()
        .templates(EmbeddedTemplates::new(TEMPLATES, ""))
        .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())?
        .build()?;
    app.verify_command(&command())?;
    Ok(())
}
```

`ListUnits` registers the command `list-units`, calls
`handlers::list_units__handler`, renders the registry entry `list-units`, and
runs on a naked invocation. Its `#[flag] all` parameter reads the clap argument
`all` that `command()` declares on that subcommand; `verify_command` is what
reports the two drifting apart, instead of leaving it to a `get_flag` panic on
the first invocation. `About` registers `about-this` and renders the
entry of the same name, because `name` changes the registration path and the
convention follows it. `Reload` registers `reload`, calls
`handlers::reload__handler` and renders nothing, so it needs no template.

# Output Modes

Standout supports multiple output formats through a single handler because modern CLI tools serve two masters: human operators and machine automation.

The same handler logic produces styled terminal output for eyes, plain text for logs, or structured JSON for `jq` pipelines—controlled entirely by the user's `--output` flag. This frees you from writing separate "API" and "CLI" logic.

## The OutputMode Enum

```rust
pub enum OutputMode {
    Auto,       // Auto-detect terminal capabilities
    Term,       // Always use ANSI escape codes
    Text,       // Never use ANSI codes (plain text)
    TermDebug,  // Keep style tags as [name]...[/name]
    Json,       // Serialize as JSON (skip template)
    Yaml,       // Serialize as YAML (skip template)
    Xml,        // Serialize as XML (skip template)
    Csv,        // Serialize as CSV (skip template)
}
```

Three categories:

**Templated modes** (Auto, Term, Text): Render the template, vary ANSI handling.

**Debug mode** (TermDebug): Render the template, keep tags as literals for inspection.

**Structured modes** (Json, Yaml, Xml, Csv): Skip the template entirely, serialize handler data directly.

## Auto Mode

`Auto` is the default. It queries the terminal for color support:

```rust
Term::stdout().features().colors_supported()
```

If colors are supported, Auto behaves like Term (ANSI codes applied). If not, Auto behaves like Text (tags stripped).

This detection happens at render time, not startup. Piping output to a file or another process typically disables color support, so:

```bash
myapp list              # Colors (if terminal supports)
myapp list > file.txt   # No colors (not a TTY)
myapp list | less       # No colors (pipe)
```

## The --output Flag

Standout adds a global `--output` flag accepting these values:

```bash
myapp list --output=auto        # Default
myapp list --output=term        # Force ANSI codes
myapp list --output=text        # Force plain text
myapp list --output=term-debug  # Show style tags
myapp list --output=json        # JSON serialization
myapp list --output=yaml        # YAML serialization
myapp list --output=xml         # XML serialization
myapp list --output=csv         # CSV serialization
```

The flag is global—it applies to all subcommands.

## Term vs Text

**Term**: turns every resolved style tag into ANSI escape codes, including
when the destination is a pipe rather than a terminal:

```bash
myapp list --output=term > colored.txt
```

Useful when you want to preserve colors for later display (e.g., `less -R`).

A `term` request is unconditional, and the environment's color conventions do
not override it: `NO_COLOR=1 myapp list --output=term` still emits ANSI, the
same way `CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 myapp list --output=text` still emits none. `auto`
is the only mode the environment reaches, and it reaches it through one value:
the destination's reported color capability. `auto` resolves to `term` when
that capability is reported and to `text` when it is not. `NO_COLOR` and
`TERM=dumb` suppress the capability, so they turn `auto` plain;
`CLICOLOR_FORCE` is not part of that capability probe, so it never turns `auto`
into `term`.

**Text**: removes Standout's own style tags and adds no ANSI of its own:

```bash
myapp list --output=text
```

Useful for clean output regardless of terminal capabilities, or when processing output with other tools.

Neither `term` nor `text` touches ANSI bytes that a handler or template
writes literally into the rendered text — the framework does not sanitize
those bytes and does not promise to. A caller that needs them gone strips
them itself.

`term-debug` (which shows tags as `[name]...[/name]` rather than resolving
them) is internal: its tag vocabulary and exact spelling may change in any
release, so don't build automation against its output the way you might
against `term` or `text`.

## TermDebug Mode

TermDebug preserves style tags instead of converting them:

```text
Template: [title]Hello[/title]
Output:   [title]Hello[/title]
```

Use cases:

- Debugging template issues
- Verifying style tag placement
- Automated testing of template output

Unlike Term mode, unknown tags don't get the `?` marker in TermDebug.
TermDebug shows tag placement; it does not check whether a tag has a matching
style definition. Use `validate_template` when validation is required.

## Structured Modes

Structured modes bypass the template entirely. Handler data is serialized directly:

```rust
#[derive(Serialize)]
struct ListOutput {
    items: Vec<Item>,
    total: usize,
}

fn list_handler(...) -> HandlerResult<ListOutput> {
    Ok(Output::Render(ListOutput { items, total: items.len() }))
}
```

```bash
myapp list --output=json
```

```json
{
  "items": [...],
  "total": 42
}
```

Same handler, same types—different output format. This enables:

- Machine-readable output for scripts
- Integration with other tools (`jq`, etc.)
- API-like behavior from CLI apps

### CSV Output

Normal `App` dispatch flattens the serializable handler data automatically for
CSV. That is the same handler data used by the other structured modes; handlers
should not inspect the requested mode or return a CSV-specific shape.

The standalone rendering API also supports direct `FlatDataSpec` rendering when
a caller needs explicit columns and headers:

```rust
use standout::tabular::{Column, FlatDataSpec, Width};
use standout::OutputMode;
use standout_render::render_auto_with_spec;

let spec = FlatDataSpec::builder()
    .column(Column::new(Width::Fixed(10)).key("name").header("Name"))
    .column(Column::new(Width::Fixed(10)).key("meta.role").header("Role"))
    .build();

render_auto_with_spec(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Csv, Some(&spec))?
```

The `key` field uses dot notation for nested paths (`"meta.role"` extracts `data["meta"]["role"]`).

When a command's canonical response is an object containing the CSV rows,
attach a presentation-layer projection through `CommandConfig`:

```rust
use serde_json::json;
use standout::cli::FnHandler;
use standout::tabular::{Column, Width};
use standout::{CsvProjection, StructuredOutputProjection};

let projection = StructuredOutputProjection::csv(
    CsvProjection::builder("items")
        .column(Column::new(Width::default()).key("language").header("LANGUAGE"))
        .column(Column::new(Width::default()).key("code").header("CODE"))
        .derived_column(
            Column::new(Width::default()).header("NET"),
            |row, _root| json!(
                row["code"].as_i64().unwrap_or(0)
                    - row["comments"].as_i64().unwrap_or(0)
            ),
        )
        .synthetic_row(|root| json!({
            "language": "TOTAL",
            "code": root["totals"]["code"],
            "comments": root["totals"]["comments"]
        }))
        .conditional_row(|root| {
            (root["skipped"].as_u64().unwrap_or(0) > 0)
                .then(|| json!({ "language": "SKIPPED" }))
        })
        .build(),
);

App::builder().command_with("summary", FnHandler::new(summary_handler), |config| {
    config.structured_output_projection(projection)
})?;
```

Direct-column dot paths are resolved against each selected row. Derived
columns receive both the current row and the root response. Synthetic-row
callbacks receive the root response and run in registration order. Column
ordering, headers, and `null_repr` use the existing `FlatDataSpec` behavior.

The projection applies only to CSV. Text and terminal modes still use the
template, while JSON, YAML, and XML serialize the canonical response. In the
pipeline, post-dispatch hooks run before projection and post-output hooks run
after it; `run`, `run_with`, output-file handling, and final emission
therefore all observe the same projected CSV.

See [Introduction to Tabular](../crates/render/guides/intro-to-tabular.md) for
tabular specifications and layout.

## File Output

The `--output-file-path` flag redirects output to a file:

```bash
myapp list --output-file-path=results.txt
myapp list --output=json --output-file-path=data.json
```

Behavior:

- Text output: written to file, nothing printed to stdout
- Binary output: written to the requested file instead of stdout
- Silent output: no-op

After writing to file, stdout output is suppressed to prevent double-printing.

## Customizing Flags

Rename or disable the flags via `AppBuilder`:

```rust
App::builder()
    .output_flag(Some("format"))       // --format instead of --output
    .output_file_flag(Some("out"))     // --out instead of --output-file-path
    .build()?
```

```rust
App::builder()
    .no_output_flag()                  // Disable --output entirely
    .no_output_file_flag()             // Disable file output
    .build()?
```

## Keep Output Mode Out of Handlers

Output mode is a rendering concern and is deliberately absent from
`CommandContext`. A handler should return the same serializable data regardless
of whether the caller selected terminal, text, or structured output. If a
command's behavior genuinely differs, model that as an explicit command or
argument rather than an implicit presentation-mode branch.

## Rendering Without CLI

For standalone rendering with explicit mode:

```rust
use standout::{render_auto, OutputMode};

// Renders template for Term/Text, serializes for Json/Yaml
let output = render_auto(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Json)?;
```

The "auto" in `render_auto` refers to template-vs-serialize dispatch, not color detection.

For full control over both output mode and color mode:

```rust
use standout::{render_with_mode, ColorMode};

let output = render_with_mode(
    template,
    &data,
    &theme,
    OutputMode::Term,
    ColorMode::Dark,
)?;
```

# Error Handling

Standout owns the shell adapter: handlers and hooks return errors as data, and
`App::run` performs the final stderr write and process exit. Ordinary handler,
hook, render, pipe, and final-write failures use status `1`; Clap usage failures
use status `2`.

## Ordinary application errors

Return ordinary errors through `HandlerResult` with `?`. Standout formats the
message as `Error: {error}` — the error's own `Display` text after that fixed
prefix — reports it under `RunErrorKind::Handler`, and exits with status `1`:

```rust
fn handler(_matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<View> {
    let view = load_view()?;
    Ok(Output::Render(view))
}
```

A hook error is framed differently today: `Hook error: {error}` under
`RunErrorKind::Hook(phase)`. A handler failure and a hook failure therefore
read as two distinct diagnostics rather than one shared shape. Settling on a
single framing for both is tracked in issue #357, in the ROB06 adopter-seams
epic; until then, treat today's wording as an implementation detail rather
than something to match against in tests.

Do not print or call `process::exit` from handlers. This keeps capture APIs,
`TestHarness`, output ownership, and real process behavior on the same seam.

## Preserving an authoritative external failure

Use `ExternalFailure` only when another operation owns the status and diagnostic
contract, such as a delegated Git invocation. Construction rejects status `0`.
The diagnostic is a verbatim stderr payload: Standout adds no `Error:` prefix
and no trailing newline.

```rust
use standout::cli::{ExternalFailure, HandlerResult};

fn handler(_matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<View> {
    let output = run_git()?;
    if !output.status.success() {
        let status = output.status.code().and_then(|code| u8::try_from(code).ok()).unwrap_or(1);
        let diagnostic = String::from_utf8_lossy(&output.stderr).into_owned();
        return Err(ExternalFailure::new(status, diagnostic)?.into());
    }
    Ok(Output::Render(to_view(output)))
}
```

A supported pre-dispatch check uses the same `ExternalFailure` interface:

```rust
Hooks::new().pre_dispatch(|_matches, _ctx| {
    let failure = ExternalFailure::new(128, "fatal: repository not found\n")
        .expect("128 is nonzero");
    Err(HookError::pre_dispatch_external(failure))
})
```

The escape hatch is not an error-mapping registry. Wrapping an ordinary error
does not change its status, and external declarations are not recognized from
post-dispatch or post-output hooks. Attach an underlying cause with
`ExternalFailure::with_source` when one exists.

Capture callers match `result.outcome()` / `into_outcome()` as
`DispatchResult::Error`, then inspect `RunErrorKind::External`,
`error.exit_status()`, and `error.as_str()`. See
[Execution Outcomes](./execution-outcomes.md) and [Testing](./testing.md).

1	# Execution Outcomes
2	
3	Standout carries shell semantics as typed data from argument parsing through
4	dispatch, rendering, hooks, output files, and final writes. Applications can let
5	`App::run` own output without losing the distinction between a usage error and a
6	runtime failure.
7	
8	## Status and streams
9	
10	| Outcome | Stream used by `run()` | Status |
11	| --- | --- | --- |
12	| Help or version | stdout | `0` |
13	| Successful rendered text or binary | stdout | `0` |
14	| `Output::Silent` | none | `0` |
15	| `--output-file-path` success | file only | `0` |
16	| Artifact written to a file | bytes to the file, report to stdout | `0` |
17	| Artifact written to stdout | bytes to stdout, report to stderr | `0` |
18	| Artifact with no selectable destination | stderr | `1` |
19	| Clap usage error | stderr | `2` |
20	| Handler, hook, render, pipe, or write failure | stderr | `1` |
21	| Application-declared external failure | stderr | exact declared nonzero status |
22	
23	Framework warning flushing happens after the primary output and does not replace
24	its status. Warnings cover non-fatal framework-owned setup, resource-loading,
25	and accepted-input diagnostics, including answer-sheet parse warnings that do
26	not reject a questionnaire submission. A final text or binary write failure does
27	replace a successful status with `1`, except that `BrokenPipe` while writing
28	final rendered command text to stdout is successful early consumer termination.
29	
30	## Capturing typed metadata
31	
32	`run_with` keeps output in-process and returns `CompletedRun`: the dispatch
33	outcome plus any framework warnings collected during the run. `Deref` keeps
34	string-oriented accessors and typed methods (`exit_status()`, `success_kind()`,
35	`error_kind()`) working on the wrapper. Pattern matching needs `outcome()` or
36	`into_outcome()`, because `CompletedRun` is not the variant enum.
37	
38	```rust
39	use standout::cli::{
40	    CompletedRun, DispatchResult, ExitStatus, OutputKind, RunError, RunErrorKind, SuccessKind,
41	};
42	use standout::{InputSources, TargetProperties};
43	
44	let result = app.run_with(
45	    command,
46	    args,
47	    TargetProperties::detect(),
48	    InputSources::from_process(),
49	);
50	let _ = result.warnings();
51	
52	match result.outcome() {
53	    DispatchResult::Handled(output) => println!("{}", output),
54	    DispatchResult::Binary(bytes, filename) => consume(bytes, filename),
55	    DispatchResult::Artifact(run) => {
56	        use std::io::{self, Write};
57	        if run.destination().is_stdout() {
58	            let mut stdout = io::stdout();
59	            stdout.write_all(run.bytes()).and_then(|()| stdout.flush()).map_err(|error| {
60	                RunError::new(
61	                    format!("Error writing artifact stdout: {}", error),
62	                    RunErrorKind::FinalWrite(OutputKind::Artifact),
63	                )
64	            })?;
65	            if let Some(report) = run.report().filter(|r| !r.is_empty()) {
66	                let mut stderr = io::stderr();
67	                writeln!(stderr, "{}", report).and_then(|()| stderr.flush()).map_err(|error| {
68	                    RunError::new(
69	                        format!("Error writing artifact report: {}", error),
70	                        RunErrorKind::FinalWrite(OutputKind::Artifact),
71	                    )
72	                })?;
73	            }
74	        } else if let Some(report) = run.report().filter(|r| !r.is_empty()) {
75	            let mut stdout = io::stdout();
76	            writeln!(stdout, "{}", report).and_then(|()| stdout.flush()).map_err(|error| {
77	                RunError::new(
78	                    format!("Error writing artifact report: {}", error),
79	                    RunErrorKind::FinalWrite(OutputKind::Artifact),
80	                )
81	            })?;
82	        }
83	    }
84	    DispatchResult::Error(error) => eprintln!("{}", error),
85	    DispatchResult::NoMatch(_matches) => {}
86	    DispatchResult::Silent => {}
87	    _ => {}
88	}
89	
90	assert_eq!(result.exit_status(), Some(ExitStatus::SUCCESS));
91	assert_eq!(result.success_kind(), Some(SuccessKind::Command));
92	assert_eq!(result.error_kind(), None);
93	```
94	
95	Use `into_outcome()` when the fallback needs owned `ArgMatches`
96	(`DispatchResult::NoMatch(matches)`).
97	
98	`RunOutput` and `RunError` dereference to `str`, implement `Display`, and expose
99	`as_str()` / `into_string()` for callers that used the tuple payloads as text.
100	`RunOutput::kind()` names a success the same way: `Command` for a handler's
101	output, `ClapHelp` / `ClapVersion` for a help or version display, and
102	`PagedHelp` for a `help --page` display — the text is identical, but the kind
103	tells a printing caller the user asked for a pager.
104	`RunError::kind()` identifies `ClapUsage`, `Handler`, `Hook(phase)`, `Render`, or
105	`FinalWrite(Text|Binary|Artifact)`. `External` identifies the narrow
106	application-declared external path; its `exit_status()` is the exact declared
107	nonzero status and its text is the verbatim diagnostic payload.
108	
109	## No-match is a handoff, not an error
110	
111	`DispatchResult::NoMatch` retains the parsed `ArgMatches` for partial adoption. It has
112	no framework exit status: `exit_status()` returns `None`, `run()` returns
113	`false`, and Standout emits nothing. The fallback dispatcher still owns that
114	command and its eventual status.

116	The reverse direction never hands off. Before parsing, `run` and
117	`run_with` check every registered path against the clap `Command`: a
118	handler registered under a path the CLI declares no subcommand for is
119	unreachable — no invocation can name it and no fallback owns it, since the app
120	did register a handler. That returns `DispatchResult::Error` naming the
121	registered path, and the clap spelling too when the two differ only by `-`
122	versus `_` (`list_units` registered against a CLI declaring `list-units`).

124	
125	That check reads canonical command names only. Clap resolves an alias to the
126	command it names before `ArgMatches` reports it, so dispatch never sees the
127	alias: a handler registered as `ls` against `Command::new("list").alias("ls")`
128	is reached by neither spelling and is reported as unreachable. Registering
129	`list` is what makes both `list` and `ls` run the handler.
130	
131	## Framework-owned final writes
132	
133	`run()` writes successful text and binary bytes to stdout, diagnostics to
134	stderr, and exits with the typed non-zero status when execution fails. The one
135	exception is a paged help display (`SuccessKind::PagedHelp`), which goes to the

138	downstream pipe is not an error only for final rendered command text:

140	writes and artifact report writes keep their typed final-write failures. The
141	suggested filename on binary output remains available to capture callers; use
142	`--output-file-path` when the framework should write either text or binary to a
143	file instead of stdout.
144	
145	Capture APIs do not perform the final stdout/stderr write, but file redirection
146	is part of dispatch and therefore reports typed `FinalWrite` failures directly.
147	External failures are never redirected to an output file: they remain stderr
148	diagnostics when `run()` performs the final write.
149	
150	Capture-mode runs drain framework warnings instead of rendering them. The raw
151	capture path stores the batch in `standout-render`'s warning collector, and
152	`standout-test::TestHarness` exposes the batch through `TestResult::warnings()`
153	so tests can assert warning content deterministically.
154	
155	## Compound artifacts
156	
157	`Output::Artifact` extends the framework-owned write to commands that also have
158	something to say about it. The application returns bytes, an optional suggested
159	destination, and an optional report; Standout selects the destination, writes,
160	and only then renders the report with a receipt naming where the bytes landed.
161	Ordering is the guarantee: a failed write produces `FinalWrite(Artifact)` and no

163	appeared.

166	destination policy, the report envelope, and the artifact-to-stdout report

# Execution Outcomes

Standout carries shell semantics as typed data from argument parsing through
dispatch, rendering, hooks, output files, and final writes. Applications can let
`App::run` own output without losing the distinction between a usage error and a
runtime failure.

## Status and streams

| Outcome | Stream used by `run()` | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Help or version | stdout | `0` |
| Successful rendered text or binary | stdout | `0` |
| `Output::Silent` | none | `0` |
| `--output-file-path` success | file only | `0` |
| Artifact written to a file | bytes to the file, report to stdout | `0` |
| Artifact written to stdout | bytes to stdout, report to stderr | `0` |
| Artifact with no selectable destination | stderr | `1` |
| Clap usage error | stderr | `2` |
| Handler, hook, render, pipe, or write failure | stderr | `1` |
| Application-declared external failure | stderr | exact declared nonzero status |

Framework warning flushing happens after the primary output and does not replace
its status. Warnings cover non-fatal framework-owned setup, resource-loading,
and accepted-input diagnostics, including answer-sheet parse warnings that do
not reject a questionnaire submission. A final text or binary write failure does
replace a successful status with `1`, except that `BrokenPipe` while writing
final rendered command text to stdout is successful early consumer termination.

## Capturing typed metadata

`run_with` keeps output in-process and returns `CompletedRun`: the dispatch
outcome plus any framework warnings collected during the run. `Deref` keeps
string-oriented accessors and typed methods (`exit_status()`, `success_kind()`,
`error_kind()`) working on the wrapper. Pattern matching needs `outcome()` or
`into_outcome()`, because `CompletedRun` is not the variant enum.

```rust
use standout::cli::{
    CompletedRun, DispatchResult, ExitStatus, OutputKind, RunError, RunErrorKind, SuccessKind,
};
use standout::{InputSources, TargetProperties};

let result = app.run_with(
    command,
    args,
    TargetProperties::detect(),
    InputSources::from_process(),
);
let _ = result.warnings();

match result.outcome() {
    DispatchResult::Handled(output) => println!("{}", output),
    DispatchResult::Binary(bytes, filename) => consume(bytes, filename),
    DispatchResult::Artifact(run) => {
        use std::io::{self, Write};
        if run.destination().is_stdout() {
            let mut stdout = io::stdout();
            stdout.write_all(run.bytes()).and_then(|()| stdout.flush()).map_err(|error| {
                RunError::new(
                    format!("Error writing artifact stdout: {}", error),
                    RunErrorKind::FinalWrite(OutputKind::Artifact),
                )
            })?;
            if let Some(report) = run.report().filter(|r| !r.is_empty()) {
                let mut stderr = io::stderr();
                writeln!(stderr, "{}", report).and_then(|()| stderr.flush()).map_err(|error| {
                    RunError::new(
                        format!("Error writing artifact report: {}", error),
                        RunErrorKind::FinalWrite(OutputKind::Artifact),
                    )
                })?;
            }
        } else if let Some(report) = run.report().filter(|r| !r.is_empty()) {
            let mut stdout = io::stdout();
            writeln!(stdout, "{}", report).and_then(|()| stdout.flush()).map_err(|error| {
                RunError::new(
                    format!("Error writing artifact report: {}", error),
                    RunErrorKind::FinalWrite(OutputKind::Artifact),
                )
            })?;
        }
    }
    DispatchResult::Error(error) => eprintln!("{}", error),
    DispatchResult::NoMatch(_matches) => {}
    DispatchResult::Silent => {}
    _ => {}
}

assert_eq!(result.exit_status(), Some(ExitStatus::SUCCESS));
assert_eq!(result.success_kind(), Some(SuccessKind::Command));
assert_eq!(result.error_kind(), None);
```

Use `into_outcome()` when the fallback needs owned `ArgMatches`
(`DispatchResult::NoMatch(matches)`).

`RunOutput` and `RunError` dereference to `str`, implement `Display`, and expose
`as_str()` / `into_string()` for callers that used the tuple payloads as text.
`RunOutput::kind()` names a success the same way: `Command` for a handler's
output, `ClapHelp` / `ClapVersion` for a help or version display, and
`PagedHelp` for a `help --page` display — the text is identical, but the kind
tells a printing caller the user asked for a pager.
`RunError::kind()` identifies `ClapUsage`, `Handler`, `Hook(phase)`, `Render`, or
`FinalWrite(Text|Binary|Artifact)`. `External` identifies the narrow
application-declared external path; its `exit_status()` is the exact declared
nonzero status and its text is the verbatim diagnostic payload.

## No-match is a handoff, not an error

`DispatchResult::NoMatch` retains the parsed `ArgMatches` for partial adoption. It has
no framework exit status: `exit_status()` returns `None`, `run()` returns
`false`, and Standout emits nothing. The fallback dispatcher still owns that
command and its eventual status.

The reverse direction never hands off. Before parsing, `run` and
`run_with` check every registered path against the clap `Command`: a
handler registered under a path the CLI declares no subcommand for is
unreachable — no invocation can name it and no fallback owns it, since the app
did register a handler. That returns `DispatchResult::Error` naming the
registered path, and the clap spelling too when the two differ only by `-`
versus `_` (`list_units` registered against a CLI declaring `list-units`).
`App::verify_command` reports the same mismatch at setup time.

That check reads canonical command names only. Clap resolves an alias to the
command it names before `ArgMatches` reports it, so dispatch never sees the
alias: a handler registered as `ls` against `Command::new("list").alias("ls")`
is reached by neither spelling and is reported as unreachable. Registering
`list` is what makes both `list` and `ls` run the handler.

## Framework-owned final writes

`run()` writes successful text and binary bytes to stdout, diagnostics to
stderr, and exits with the typed non-zero status when execution fails. The one
exception is a paged help display (`SuccessKind::PagedHelp`), which goes to the
pager instead; if no pager is available it falls back to stdout, so help is
never lost. A closed
downstream pipe is not an error only for final rendered command text:
`BrokenPipe` there means the consumer stopped reading early. Binary stdout
writes and artifact report writes keep their typed final-write failures. The
suggested filename on binary output remains available to capture callers; use
`--output-file-path` when the framework should write either text or binary to a
file instead of stdout.

Capture APIs do not perform the final stdout/stderr write, but file redirection
is part of dispatch and therefore reports typed `FinalWrite` failures directly.
External failures are never redirected to an output file: they remain stderr
diagnostics when `run()` performs the final write.

Capture-mode runs drain framework warnings instead of rendering them. The raw
capture path stores the batch in `standout-render`'s warning collector, and
`standout-test::TestHarness` exposes the batch through `TestResult::warnings()`
so tests can assert warning content deterministically.

## Compound artifacts

`Output::Artifact` extends the framework-owned write to commands that also have
something to say about it. The application returns bytes, an optional suggested
destination, and an optional report; Standout selects the destination, writes,
and only then renders the report with a receipt naming where the bytes landed.
Ordering is the guarantee: a failed write produces `FinalWrite(Artifact)` and no
report at all, so a success message can never promise a file that never
appeared.

See [Handler Contract](../crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md) for the
destination policy, the report envelope, and the artifact-to-stdout report
channel.
