1	# The Handler Contract
2	
3	Handlers are shell adapters: they map parsed CLI input to application calls and
4	return serializable CLI-owned view data. Keep reusable behavior in a CLI-free
5	library. The handler contract is designed to be **explicit** rather than
6	permissive, so adapters remain testable and decoupled from output formatting.
7	
8	---
9	
10	## Quick Start: The `#[handler]` Macro
11	
12	For most handlers, use the `#[handler]` macro to write typed adapter functions:
13	
14	```rust,ignore
15	use standout_macros::handler;
16	
17	#[handler]
18	pub fn list(#[flag] all: bool, #[arg] limit: Option<usize>) -> Result<Vec<Item>, anyhow::Error> {
19	    storage::list(all, limit)
20	}
21	```
22	
23	The macro leaves `list` alone and adds three items beside it:
24	
25	| Item | What it is |
26	| --- | --- |
27	| `list__handler(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext)` | reads the arguments out of `ArgMatches` and calls `list`. It returns **the annotated return type verbatim** — here `Result<Vec<Item>, anyhow::Error>`, not `HandlerResult<Vec<Item>>` |
28	| `list__expected_args() -> Vec<ExpectedArg>` | what `App::verify_command` reads |
29	| `list_Handler` | a unit struct implementing [`Handler`](#the-handler-trait) — **the registrable item** |
30	
31	The `Result<T, E>` to `Output::Render` wrap happens inside `list_Handler`'s
32	`Handler::handle`, which calls `IntoHandlerResult::into_handler_result` on
33	whatever `list__handler` returned. It is not applied by `list__handler` itself.
34	Only registration of `list_Handler` runs that wrap. `#[derive(Dispatch)]` does
35	not reach the trait object at all: it registers the closure
36	`handlers::list__handler` through `GroupBuilder::command_with`, so nothing
37	calls `Handler::handle` and the annotated return type has to be a
38	`HandlerResult` shape already. That is the difference the next two tables
39	spell out.
40	
41	The un-suffixed `handlers::list` is not registrable — it has the wrong
42	signature by design, so that a test can call it directly. Which of the other
43	two items you register depends on the method:
44	
45	| Method | What it takes | What to pass |
46	| --- | --- | --- |
47	| `AppBuilder::command_with` | `impl Handler` | `handlers::list_Handler` |
48	| `GroupBuilder::command` / `command_with`, and therefore `#[derive(Dispatch)]` | a closure returning `HandlerResult<T>` | `handlers::list__handler` |
49	
50	That second row constrains the return type, and it is the one place the two
51	registration paths genuinely differ. `list__handler` returns the annotated type
52	verbatim, so it satisfies `HandlerResult<T>` only when the function was written
53	`-> Result<Output<T>, E>` (or `-> Result<(), E>`, whose wrapper returns
54	`HandlerResult<()>`). **A handler annotated `-> Result<T, E>` cannot be
55	registered through `#[derive(Dispatch)]`**: expansion fails with `expected
56	list__handler to return Result<Output<_>, Error>, but it returns Result<Items,
57	Error>`. Write it `-> Result<Output<T>, E>`, or register `list_Handler` through
58	`AppBuilder::command_with`, where `Handler::handle` applies the wrap for you.
59	
60	The three return shapes, and the original functions still being callable:
61	
62	```rust
63	use standout::cli::{CommandContext, Output};
64	use standout::handler;
65	
66	#[derive(serde::Serialize)]
67	pub struct Items {
68	    pub names: Vec<String>,
69	}
70	
71	/// `Handler::Output` is `Items`; `handle` wraps the value in `Output::Render`.
72	#[handler]
73	pub fn list(#[flag] all: bool) -> Result<Items, anyhow::Error> {
74	    let mut names = vec!["ssh".to_string()];
75	    if all {
76	        names.push("cron".to_string());
77	    }
78	    Ok(Items { names })
79	}
80	
81	/// `Handler::Output` is `Items`; the `Output` passes through untouched.
82	#[handler]
83	pub fn about(#[ctx] _ctx: &CommandContext) -> Result<Output<Items>, anyhow::Error> {
84	    Ok(Output::Render(Items { names: vec!["unitctl".to_string()] }))
85	}
86	
87	/// `Handler::Output` is `()`; `handle` produces `Output::Silent`.
88	#[handler]
89	pub fn reload(#[flag] _force: bool) -> Result<(), anyhow::Error> {
90	    Ok(())
91	}
92	
93	fn main() {
94	    // No ArgMatches, no dispatcher: the annotated function is what a unit test calls.
95	    assert_eq!(list(true).unwrap().names, ["ssh", "cron"]);
96	    reload(false).unwrap();
97	}
98	```
99	
100	Every `#[dispatch(…)]` and `#[handler]` attribute is listed in the
101	[`#[dispatch(…)]` and `#[handler]` reference](../../../topics/dispatch-attributes.md).
102	
103	**Parameter Annotations:**
104	
105	| Annotation            | Type              | Extraction                    |
106	| --------------------- | ----------------- | ----------------------------- |
107	| `#[flag]`             | `bool`            | `matches.get_flag("name")`    |
108	| `#[flag(name = "x")]` | `bool`            | `matches.get_flag("x")`       |
109	| `#[arg]`              | `T`               | Required argument             |
110	| `#[arg]`              | `Option<T>`       | Optional argument             |
111	| `#[arg]`              | `Vec<T>`          | Multiple values               |
112	| `#[arg(name = "x")]`  | `T`               | Argument with custom CLI name |
113	| `#[ctx]`              | `&CommandContext` | Access to context             |
114	| `#[matches]`          | `&ArgMatches`     | Raw matches (escape hatch)    |
115	
116	Without `name = "x"`, the argument id is the parameter name with underscores
117	turned into hyphens: `no_legend` reads the argument id `no-legend`. Clap's own
118	derive ids an argument by the field name it comes from, so a clap-derive
119	`no_legend` field declares `#[arg(id = "no-legend")]` to meet the handler, or
120	the handler parameter takes the field's id with `#[flag(name = "no_legend")]`.
121	`app.verify_command(&cmd)` reports the mismatch instead of leaving it to a
122	runtime `get_flag` panic. A parameter named with a raw identifier drops the
123	`r#` first, the way clap's derive drops it from a field name: `r#type` reads
124	the argument id `type`.
125	
126	**Return Type Handling:** the function must return `Result<T, E>`; the macro
127	rejects anything else with `handler must return Result<T, E>`. What `T` is
128	decides what `Handler::Output` becomes and whether anything is wrapped.
129	
130	| Annotated return type | `Handler::Output` | What `handle` produces |
131	| --- | --- | --- |
132	| `Result<T, E>` | `T` | `Ok(value)` wrapped in `Output::Render(value)` |
133	| `Result<Output<T>, E>` (that is, `HandlerResult<T>`) | `T` | the `Output` you returned, unchanged |
134	| `Result<(), E>` | `()` | `Output::Silent` |
135	
136	> **Testing:** The original function is preserved, so you can test directly: `list(true, Some(10))`.
137	
138	---
139	
140	## The Handler Trait
141	
142	```rust,ignore
143	pub trait Handler {
144	    type Output: Serialize;
145	    fn handle(&mut self, matches: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Self::Output>;
146	}
147	```
148	
149	Key characteristics:
150	
151	- **Mutable self**: `&mut self` allows direct state modification
152	- **Output must be Serialize**: Needed for JSON/YAML modes and template context
153	
154	Implementing the trait directly is useful when your handler needs internal state—database connections, configuration, caches, etc.
155	
156	### Example: Struct Handler with State
157	
158	```rust,ignore
159	use standout_dispatch::{Handler, Output, CommandContext, HandlerResult};
160	use clap::ArgMatches;
161	use serde::Serialize;
162	
163	struct CachingDatabase {
164	    connection: Connection,
165	    cache: HashMap<String, Vec<Row>>,
166	}
167	
168	impl CachingDatabase {
169	    fn query_with_cache(&mut self, sql: &str) -> Result<Vec<Row>, Error> {
170	        if let Some(cached) = self.cache.get(sql) {
171	            return Ok(cached.clone());
172	        }
173	        let result = self.connection.execute(sql)?;
174	        self.cache.insert(sql.to_string(), result.clone());
175	        Ok(result)
176	    }
177	}
178	
179	impl Handler for CachingDatabase {
180	    type Output = Vec<Row>;
181	
182	    fn handle(&mut self, matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Vec<Row>> {
183	        let query: &String = matches.get_one("query").unwrap();
184	        let rows = self.query_with_cache(query)?;  // &mut self works!
185	        Ok(Output::Render(rows))
186	    }
187	}
188	```
189	
190	---
191	
192	## Closure Handlers
193	
194	Most handlers are simple closures using `FnHandler`:
195	
196	```rust,ignore
197	use standout_dispatch::{FnHandler, Output, HandlerResult};
198	
199	let mut counter = 0;
200	
201	let handler = FnHandler::new(move |_matches, _ctx| {
202	    counter += 1;  // Mutation works!
203	    Ok(Output::Render(counter))
204	});
205	```
206	
207	The closure signature:
208	
209	```rust,ignore
210	fn(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<T>
211	where T: Serialize
212	```
213	
214	Closures are `FnMut`, allowing captured variables to be mutated.
215	
216	---
217	
218	## SimpleFnHandler (No Context Needed)
219	
220	When your handler doesn't need `CommandContext`, use `SimpleFnHandler` for a cleaner signature:
221	
222	```rust,ignore
223	use standout_dispatch::SimpleFnHandler;
224	
225	let handler = SimpleFnHandler::new(|matches| {
226	    let verbose = matches.get_flag("verbose");
227	    let items = storage::list()?;
228	    Ok(ListResult { items, verbose })
229	});
230	```
231	
232	The closure signature:
233	
234	```rust,ignore
235	fn(&ArgMatches) -> Result<T, E>
236	where T: Serialize, E: Into<anyhow::Error>
237	```
238	
239	`SimpleFnHandler` automatically wraps the result in `Output::Render` via `IntoHandlerResult`.
240	
241	---
242	
243	## IntoHandlerResult Trait
244	
245	The `IntoHandlerResult` trait enables handlers to return `Result<T, E>` directly instead of `HandlerResult<T>`:
246	
247	```rust,ignore
248	use standout_dispatch::IntoHandlerResult;
249	
250	// Before: explicit Output wrapping
251	fn list(_m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Vec<Item>> {
252	    let items = storage::list()?;
253	    Ok(Output::Render(items))
254	}
255	
256	// After: automatic conversion
257	fn list(_m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> impl IntoHandlerResult<Vec<Item>> {
258	    storage::list()  // Result<Vec<Item>, Error> auto-converts
259	}
260	```
261	
262	The trait is implemented for:
263	
264	- `Result<T, E>` where `E: Into<anyhow::Error>` → wraps `Ok(t)` in `Output::Render(t)`
265	- `HandlerResult<T>` → passes through unchanged
266	
267	This is used internally by `SimpleFnHandler` and the `#[handler]` macro.
268	
269	---
270	
271	## HandlerResult
272	
273	`HandlerResult<T>` is a standard `Result` type:
274	
275	```rust,ignore
276	pub type HandlerResult<T> = Result<Output<T>, anyhow::Error>;
277	```
278	
279	The `?` operator works naturally for error propagation:
280	
281	```rust,ignore
282	fn list_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Items> {
283	    let items = storage::load()?;           // Propagates errors
284	    let filtered = filter_items(&items)?;   // Propagates errors
285	    Ok(Output::Render(Items { filtered }))
286	}
287	```
288	
289	### Authoritative external failures
290	
291	When a handler delegates to another executable and the application's contract
292	requires that executable's exact nonzero status and stderr, return the public
293	`ExternalFailure` type through the same `HandlerResult` seam:
294	
295	```rust,ignore
296	let failure = ExternalFailure::new(128, git_stderr)?;
297	Err(failure.into())
298	```
299	
300	Construction rejects status `0`. Standout recognizes only this concrete type,
301	preserves its diagnostic verbatim, and exposes it as `RunErrorKind::External`.
302	Ordinary handler errors still use status `1`; this is not a general exit-code
303	mapping mechanism. Handlers must not print or call `process::exit` themselves.
304	
305	---
306	
307	## The Output Enum
308	
309	`Output<T>` represents what a handler produces:
310	
311	```rust,ignore
312	#[non_exhaustive]
313	pub enum Output<T: Serialize> {
314	    Render(T),
315	    Silent,
316	    Binary { data: Vec<u8>, filename: String },
317	    Artifact(Artifact<T>),
318	}
319	```
320	
321	`Output` is `#[non_exhaustive]`: matches on it need a `_` arm so later shapes
322	can be added without breaking downstream code.
323	
324	### Output::Render(T)
325	
326	The common case. Data is passed to the render function:
327	
328	```rust,ignore
329	#[derive(Serialize)]
330	struct ListResult {
331	    items: Vec<Item>,
332	    total: usize,
333	}
334	
335	fn list_handler(_m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<ListResult> {
336	    let items = storage::list()?;
337	    Ok(Output::Render(ListResult {
338	        total: items.len(),
339	        items,
340	    }))
341	}
342	```
343	
344	### Output::Silent
345	
346	No output produced. Useful for commands with side effects only:
347	
348	```rust,ignore
349	fn delete_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<()> {
350	    let id: &String = matches.get_one("id").unwrap();
351	    storage::delete(id)?;
352	    Ok(Output::Silent)
353	}
354	```
355	
356	Silent behavior:
357	
358	- Post-output hooks still receive `RenderedOutput::Silent`
359	- Render function is not called
360	- Nothing prints to stdout
361	
362	### Output::Binary
363	
364	Raw bytes for file output:
365	
366	```rust,ignore
367	fn export_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<()> {
368	    let data = generate_report()?;
369	    let pdf_bytes = render_to_pdf(&data)?;
370	
371	    Ok(Output::Binary {
372	        data: pdf_bytes,
373	        filename: "report.pdf".into(),
374	    })
375	}
376	```
377	
378	Binary output bypasses the render function entirely.
379	
380	The filename is a **hint for the caller**, not permission to write. Without
381	`--output-file-path`, `run()` sends the bytes to stdout and touches no file. If
382	you want the framework to write the suggested destination, use `Output::Artifact`
383	— that opt-in is the whole difference between the two shapes.
384	
385	### Output::Artifact
386	
387	Owned bytes plus an application-owned report, for commands that produce a file
388	*and* have something to say about it. `Output::Binary` cannot carry a report,
389	and nothing renders after its write, so a command that wants to say "exported 12
390	rows to /tmp/report.csv (2 warnings)" would otherwise have to write the file
391	itself — pulling destination policy back into the application core.
392	
393	```rust,ignore
394	use standout::cli::{Artifact, HandlerResult, Output};
395	
396	#[derive(Serialize)]
397	struct ExportReport {
398	    exported: usize,
399	    warnings: Vec<Warning>,
400	}
401	
402	fn export_handler(_m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<ExportReport> {
403	    let export = core::export_csv()?;   // bytes + facts, no filesystem
404	
405	    Ok(Output::Artifact(
406	        Artifact::new(export.csv)
407	            .suggest_destination(export.suggested_filename)
408	            .with_report(ExportReport {
409	                exported: export.rows,
410	                warnings: export.warnings,
411	            }),
412	    ))
413	}
414	```
415	
416	Who owns what:
417	
418	| Concern | Owner |
419	| --- | --- |
420	| Artifact bytes | Application |
421	| Suggested destination | Application (a suggestion) |
422	| Semantic report and warning taxonomy | Application |
423	| Destination selection | Framework |
424	| The write and its failure | Framework |
425	| Receipt (completed destination) | Framework |
426	
427	#### Destination policy
428	
429	Standout selects the destination deterministically:
430	
431	1. the explicit `--output-file-path` override;
432	2. the artifact's `suggest_destination(...)`, if the application opted in;
433	3. stdout, if the application opted in with `allow_stdout()`.
434	
435	If none applies, the run fails with `FinalWrite(Artifact)` rather than inventing
436	a file or dropping the bytes. All three steps share that one failure path.
437	
438	#### Write first, report second
439	
440	Standout writes, then renders the report from a fixed envelope:
441	
442	```json
443	{
444	  "report": { "exported": 12, "warnings": [] },
445	  "receipt": { "destination": "/tmp/report.csv", "stdout": false, "byte_count": 480 }
446	}
447	```
448	
449	So a template can say what only the framework knows:
450	
451	```jinja
452	Exported {{ report.exported }} rows to {{ receipt.destination }}
453	```
454	
455	The envelope shape is fixed (`report` + `receipt`) whatever the report's type,
456	so no application key can collide with the receipt. Structured modes serialize
457	the same envelope. A failed write renders nothing: success cannot outrun the
458	write that justifies it.
459	
460	#### The report channel
461	
462	Mixing a report into the bytes would corrupt them, so the channel follows the
463	destination:
464	
465	| Artifact destination | Report goes to |
466	| --- | --- |
467	| File | stdout |
468	| Stdout (`allow_stdout()`) | stderr |
469	
470	#### Hooks and artifacts
471	
472	Post-dispatch hooks see the report as ordinary handler data. Post-output hooks
473	see `RenderedOutput::Artifact` and can still transform the bytes or the report
474	via `as_artifact_mut()`. Hooks never perform the write — that stays framework-
475	owned, which is what keeps the failure path single and the report honest.
476	
477	Bytes are owned; streaming is deliberately not part of this contract.
478	
479	---
480	
481	## CommandContext
482	
483	`CommandContext` provides execution environment information and state access:
484	
485	```rust,ignore
486	pub struct CommandContext {
487	    pub command_path: Vec<String>,
488	    pub app_state: Rc<Extensions>,
489	    pub extensions: Extensions,
490	}
491	```
492	
493	**command_path**: The subcommand chain as a vector, e.g., `["db", "migrate"]`. Useful for logging or conditional logic.
494	
495	**app_state**: Shared, immutable state configured at app build time via `AppBuilder::app_state()`. Wrapped in `Arc` for cheap cloning. Use for database connections, configuration, API clients.
496	
497	**extensions**: Per-request, mutable state injected by pre-dispatch hooks. Use for user sessions, request IDs, computed values.
498	
499	> For comprehensive coverage of state management, see [App State and Extensions](app-state.md).
500	
501	---
502	
503	## State Access: App State vs Extensions
504	
505	Handlers access state through two distinct mechanisms with different semantics:
506	
507	| Aspect         | `ctx.app_state`               | `ctx.extensions`           |
508	| -------------- | ----------------------------- | -------------------------- |
509	| **Mutability** | Immutable (`&`)               | Mutable (`&mut`)           |
510	| **Lifetime**   | App lifetime                  | Per-request                |
511	| **Set by**     | `AppBuilder::app_state()`     | Pre-dispatch hooks         |
512	| **Use for**    | Database, Config, API clients | User sessions, request IDs |
513	
514	### App State (Shared Resources)
515	
516	Configure long-lived resources at build time:
517	
518	```rust,ignore
519	App::builder()
520	    .app_state(Database::connect()?)
521	    .app_state(Config::load()?)
522	    .command("list", list_handler, template)?
523	    .build()?
524	```
525	
526	Access in handlers via `ctx.app_state`:
527	
528	```rust,ignore
529	fn list_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Vec<Item>> {
530	    let db = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?;
531	    let config = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Config>()?;
532	
533	    let items = db.query_items(config.max_results)?;
534	    Ok(Output::Render(items))
535	}
536	```
537	
538	### Extensions (Per-Request State)
539	
540	Pre-dispatch hooks inject request-scoped state:
541	
542	```rust,ignore
543	use standout_dispatch::{Hooks, HookError};
544	
545	struct UserScope { user_id: String, permissions: Vec<String> }
546	
547	let hooks = Hooks::new()
548	    .pre_dispatch(|matches, ctx| {
549	        // Can read app_state to set up per-request state
550	        let db = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?;
551	
552	        let user_id = matches.get_one::<String>("user").unwrap().clone();
553	        let permissions = db.get_permissions(&user_id)?;
554	
555	        ctx.extensions.insert(UserScope { user_id, permissions });
556	        Ok(())
557	    });
558	```
559	
560	Handlers retrieve from extensions:
561	
562	```rust,ignore
563	fn list_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Vec<Item>> {
564	    let db = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?;       // shared
565	    let scope = ctx.extensions.get_required::<UserScope>()?;  // per-request
566	
567	    let items = db.list_for_user(&scope.user_id)?;
568	    Ok(Output::Render(items))
569	}
570	```
571	
572	### Extensions API
573	
574	Both `app_state` and `extensions` use the same `Extensions` type with these methods:
575	
576	| Method              | Description                                     |
577	| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
578	| `insert<T>(value)`  | Insert a value, returns previous if any         |
579	| `get<T>()`          | Get immutable reference, returns `Option<&T>`   |
580	| `get_required<T>()` | Get reference or return error if missing        |
581	| `get_mut<T>()`      | Get mutable reference, returns `Option<&mut T>` |
582	| `remove<T>()`       | Remove and return value                         |
583	| `contains<T>()`     | Check if type exists                            |
584	| `len()`             | Number of stored values                         |
585	| `is_empty()`        | True if no values stored                        |
586	| `clear()`           | Remove all values                               |
587	
588	Use `get_required` for mandatory dependencies (fails fast with clear error), `get` for optional ones.
589	
590	### When to Use Which
591	
592	**Use App State for:**
593	
594	- Database connections — expensive to create, should be pooled
595	- Configuration — loaded once at startup
596	- API clients — shared HTTP clients with connection pooling
597	
598	**Use Extensions for:**
599	
600	- User context — current user, session, permissions
601	- Request metadata — request ID, timing, correlation ID
602	- Transient state — data computed by one hook, used by handler
603	
604	### The Two-State Pattern
605	
606	The separation exists because:
607	
608	1. **Closure capture doesn't work with `#[derive(Dispatch)]`** — macro-generated dispatch calls handlers with a fixed signature
609	2. **App-level resources shouldn't be created per-request** — database pools and config are expensive
610	3. **Per-request state needs mutable injection** — hooks compute values at runtime
611	
612	```rust,ignore
613	// App state: configured once at build time
614	App::builder()
615	    .app_state(Database::connect()?)  // Shared via Arc
616	    .hooks("users.list", Hooks::new()
617	        .pre_dispatch(|matches, ctx| {
618	            // Extensions: computed per-request, can use app_state
619	            let db = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?;
620	            let user = authenticate(matches, db)?;
621	            ctx.extensions.insert(user);
622	            Ok(())
623	        }))?
624	```
625	
626	> For comprehensive coverage of state management patterns, see [App State and Extensions](app-state.md).
627	
628	---
629	
630	## Accessing CLI Arguments
631	
632	The `ArgMatches` parameter provides access to parsed arguments through clap's standard API:
633	
634	```rust,ignore
635	fn handler(matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Data> {
636	    // Flags
637	    let verbose = matches.get_flag("verbose");
638	
639	    // Required options
640	    let name: &String = matches.get_one("name").unwrap();
641	
642	    // Optional values
643	    let limit: Option<&u32> = matches.get_one("limit");
644	
645	    // Multiple values
646	    let tags: Vec<&String> = matches.get_many("tags")
647	        .map(|v| v.collect())
648	        .unwrap_or_default();
649	
650	    Ok(Output::Render(Data { ... }))
651	}
652	```
653	
654	For subcommands, you work with the `ArgMatches` for your specific command level.
655	
656	---
657	
658	## Testing Handlers
659	
660	Because handlers have explicit inputs and outputs, their adapter behavior is
661	straightforward to test directly. Test validation, filtering, and state
662	transitions through the CLI-free library instead:
663	
664	```rust,ignore
665	#[test]
666	fn test_list_handler() {
667	    let cmd = Command::new("test")
668	        .arg(Arg::new("verbose").long("verbose").action(ArgAction::SetTrue));
669	    let matches = cmd.try_get_matches_from(["test", "--verbose"]).unwrap();
670	
671	    let ctx = CommandContext {
672	        command_path: vec!["list".into()],
673	        ..Default::default()
674	    };
675	
676	    let result = list_handler(&matches, &ctx);
677	
678	    assert!(result.is_ok());
679	    if let Ok(Output::Render(data)) = result {
680	        assert!(data.verbose);
681	    }
682	}
683	```
684	
685	No mocking frameworks needed—construct `ArgMatches` with clap, create a `CommandContext`, call your handler, assert on the result.
686	
687	### Testing with App State
688	
689	When handlers depend on app_state, inject test fixtures:
690	
691	```rust,ignore
692	#[test]
693	fn test_handler_with_app_state() {
694	    use std::sync::Arc;
695	
696	    // Create test fixtures
697	    let mock_db = MockDatabase::with_items(vec![
698	        Item { id: "1", name: "Test" }
699	    ]);
700	
701	    // Build app_state with test data
702	    let mut app_state = Extensions::new();
703	    app_state.insert(mock_db);
704	
705	    let ctx = CommandContext {
706	        command_path: vec!["list".into()],
707	        app_state: Arc::new(app_state),
708	        extensions: Extensions::new(),
709	    };
710	
711	    let cmd = Command::new("test");
712	    let matches = cmd.try_get_matches_from(["test"]).unwrap();
713	
714	    let result = list_handler(&matches, &ctx);
715	    assert!(result.is_ok());
716	}
717	```
718	
719	### Testing Handlers with Mutable State
720	
721	Handler tests can verify state mutation across calls:
722	
723	```rust,ignore
724	#[test]
725	fn test_handler_state_mutation() {
726	    struct Counter { count: u32 }
727	
728	    impl Handler for Counter {
729	        type Output = u32;
730	        fn handle(&mut self, _m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<u32> {
731	            self.count += 1;
732	            Ok(Output::Render(self.count))
733	        }
734	    }
735	
736	    let mut handler = Counter { count: 0 };
737	    let cmd = Command::new("test");
738	    let matches = cmd.try_get_matches_from(["test"]).unwrap();
739	    let ctx = CommandContext {
740	        command_path: vec!["count".into()],
741	        ..Default::default()
742	    };
743	
744	    // State accumulates across calls
745	    let _ = handler.handle(&matches, &ctx);
746	    let _ = handler.handle(&matches, &ctx);
747	    let result = handler.handle(&matches, &ctx);
748	
749	    assert!(matches!(result, Ok(Output::Render(3))));
750	}
751	```
752

# The Handler Contract

Handlers are shell adapters: they map parsed CLI input to application calls and
return serializable CLI-owned view data. Keep reusable behavior in a CLI-free
library. The handler contract is designed to be **explicit** rather than
permissive, so adapters remain testable and decoupled from output formatting.

---

## Quick Start: The `#[handler]` Macro

For most handlers, use the `#[handler]` macro to write typed adapter functions:

```rust,ignore
use standout_macros::handler;

#[handler]
pub fn list(#[flag] all: bool, #[arg] limit: Option<usize>) -> Result<Vec<Item>, anyhow::Error> {
    storage::list(all, limit)
}
```

The macro leaves `list` alone and adds three items beside it:

| Item | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `list__handler(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext)` | reads the arguments out of `ArgMatches` and calls `list`. It returns **the annotated return type verbatim** — here `Result<Vec<Item>, anyhow::Error>`, not `HandlerResult<Vec<Item>>` |
| `list__expected_args() -> Vec<ExpectedArg>` | what `App::verify_command` reads |
| `list_Handler` | a unit struct implementing [`Handler`](#the-handler-trait) — **the registrable item** |

The `Result<T, E>` to `Output::Render` wrap happens inside `list_Handler`'s
`Handler::handle`, which calls `IntoHandlerResult::into_handler_result` on
whatever `list__handler` returned. It is not applied by `list__handler` itself.
Only registration of `list_Handler` runs that wrap. `#[derive(Dispatch)]` does
not reach the trait object at all: it registers the closure
`handlers::list__handler` through `GroupBuilder::command_with`, so nothing
calls `Handler::handle` and the annotated return type has to be a
`HandlerResult` shape already. That is the difference the next two tables
spell out.

The un-suffixed `handlers::list` is not registrable — it has the wrong
signature by design, so that a test can call it directly. Which of the other
two items you register depends on the method:

| Method | What it takes | What to pass |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AppBuilder::command_with` | `impl Handler` | `handlers::list_Handler` |
| `GroupBuilder::command` / `command_with`, and therefore `#[derive(Dispatch)]` | a closure returning `HandlerResult<T>` | `handlers::list__handler` |

That second row constrains the return type, and it is the one place the two
registration paths genuinely differ. `list__handler` returns the annotated type
verbatim, so it satisfies `HandlerResult<T>` only when the function was written
`-> Result<Output<T>, E>` (or `-> Result<(), E>`, whose wrapper returns
`HandlerResult<()>`). **A handler annotated `-> Result<T, E>` cannot be
registered through `#[derive(Dispatch)]`**: expansion fails with `expected
list__handler to return Result<Output<_>, Error>, but it returns Result<Items,
Error>`. Write it `-> Result<Output<T>, E>`, or register `list_Handler` through
`AppBuilder::command_with`, where `Handler::handle` applies the wrap for you.

The three return shapes, and the original functions still being callable:

```rust
use standout::cli::{CommandContext, Output};
use standout::handler;

#[derive(serde::Serialize)]
pub struct Items {
    pub names: Vec<String>,
}

/// `Handler::Output` is `Items`; `handle` wraps the value in `Output::Render`.
#[handler]
pub fn list(#[flag] all: bool) -> Result<Items, anyhow::Error> {
    let mut names = vec!["ssh".to_string()];
    if all {
        names.push("cron".to_string());
    }
    Ok(Items { names })
}

/// `Handler::Output` is `Items`; the `Output` passes through untouched.
#[handler]
pub fn about(#[ctx] _ctx: &CommandContext) -> Result<Output<Items>, anyhow::Error> {
    Ok(Output::Render(Items { names: vec!["unitctl".to_string()] }))
}

/// `Handler::Output` is `()`; `handle` produces `Output::Silent`.
#[handler]
pub fn reload(#[flag] _force: bool) -> Result<(), anyhow::Error> {
    Ok(())
}

fn main() {
    // No ArgMatches, no dispatcher: the annotated function is what a unit test calls.
    assert_eq!(list(true).unwrap().names, ["ssh", "cron"]);
    reload(false).unwrap();
}
```

Every `#[dispatch(…)]` and `#[handler]` attribute is listed in the
[`#[dispatch(…)]` and `#[handler]` reference](../../../topics/dispatch-attributes.md).

**Parameter Annotations:**

| Annotation            | Type              | Extraction                    |
| --------------------- | ----------------- | ----------------------------- |
| `#[flag]`             | `bool`            | `matches.get_flag("name")`    |
| `#[flag(name = "x")]` | `bool`            | `matches.get_flag("x")`       |
| `#[arg]`              | `T`               | Required argument             |
| `#[arg]`              | `Option<T>`       | Optional argument             |
| `#[arg]`              | `Vec<T>`          | Multiple values               |
| `#[arg(name = "x")]`  | `T`               | Argument with custom CLI name |
| `#[ctx]`              | `&CommandContext` | Access to context             |
| `#[matches]`          | `&ArgMatches`     | Raw matches (escape hatch)    |

Without `name = "x"`, the argument id is the parameter name with underscores
turned into hyphens: `no_legend` reads the argument id `no-legend`. Clap's own
derive ids an argument by the field name it comes from, so a clap-derive
`no_legend` field declares `#[arg(id = "no-legend")]` to meet the handler, or
the handler parameter takes the field's id with `#[flag(name = "no_legend")]`.
`app.verify_command(&cmd)` reports the mismatch instead of leaving it to a
runtime `get_flag` panic. A parameter named with a raw identifier drops the
`r#` first, the way clap's derive drops it from a field name: `r#type` reads
the argument id `type`.

**Return Type Handling:** the function must return `Result<T, E>`; the macro
rejects anything else with `handler must return Result<T, E>`. What `T` is
decides what `Handler::Output` becomes and whether anything is wrapped.

| Annotated return type | `Handler::Output` | What `handle` produces |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Result<T, E>` | `T` | `Ok(value)` wrapped in `Output::Render(value)` |
| `Result<Output<T>, E>` (that is, `HandlerResult<T>`) | `T` | the `Output` you returned, unchanged |
| `Result<(), E>` | `()` | `Output::Silent` |

> **Testing:** The original function is preserved, so you can test directly: `list(true, Some(10))`.

---

## The Handler Trait

```rust,ignore
pub trait Handler {
    type Output: Serialize;
    fn handle(&mut self, matches: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Self::Output>;
}
```

Key characteristics:

- **Mutable self**: `&mut self` allows direct state modification
- **Output must be Serialize**: Needed for JSON/YAML modes and template context

Implementing the trait directly is useful when your handler needs internal state—database connections, configuration, caches, etc.

### Example: Struct Handler with State

```rust,ignore
use standout_dispatch::{Handler, Output, CommandContext, HandlerResult};
use clap::ArgMatches;
use serde::Serialize;

struct CachingDatabase {
    connection: Connection,
    cache: HashMap<String, Vec<Row>>,
}

impl CachingDatabase {
    fn query_with_cache(&mut self, sql: &str) -> Result<Vec<Row>, Error> {
        if let Some(cached) = self.cache.get(sql) {
            return Ok(cached.clone());
        }
        let result = self.connection.execute(sql)?;
        self.cache.insert(sql.to_string(), result.clone());
        Ok(result)
    }
}

impl Handler for CachingDatabase {
    type Output = Vec<Row>;

    fn handle(&mut self, matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Vec<Row>> {
        let query: &String = matches.get_one("query").unwrap();
        let rows = self.query_with_cache(query)?;  // &mut self works!
        Ok(Output::Render(rows))
    }
}
```

---

## Closure Handlers

Most handlers are simple closures using `FnHandler`:

```rust,ignore
use standout_dispatch::{FnHandler, Output, HandlerResult};

let mut counter = 0;

let handler = FnHandler::new(move |_matches, _ctx| {
    counter += 1;  // Mutation works!
    Ok(Output::Render(counter))
});
```

The closure signature:

```rust,ignore
fn(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<T>
where T: Serialize
```

Closures are `FnMut`, allowing captured variables to be mutated.

---

## SimpleFnHandler (No Context Needed)

When your handler doesn't need `CommandContext`, use `SimpleFnHandler` for a cleaner signature:

```rust,ignore
use standout_dispatch::SimpleFnHandler;

let handler = SimpleFnHandler::new(|matches| {
    let verbose = matches.get_flag("verbose");
    let items = storage::list()?;
    Ok(ListResult { items, verbose })
});
```

The closure signature:

```rust,ignore
fn(&ArgMatches) -> Result<T, E>
where T: Serialize, E: Into<anyhow::Error>
```

`SimpleFnHandler` automatically wraps the result in `Output::Render` via `IntoHandlerResult`.

---

## IntoHandlerResult Trait

The `IntoHandlerResult` trait enables handlers to return `Result<T, E>` directly instead of `HandlerResult<T>`:

```rust,ignore
use standout_dispatch::IntoHandlerResult;

// Before: explicit Output wrapping
fn list(_m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Vec<Item>> {
    let items = storage::list()?;
    Ok(Output::Render(items))
}

// After: automatic conversion
fn list(_m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> impl IntoHandlerResult<Vec<Item>> {
    storage::list()  // Result<Vec<Item>, Error> auto-converts
}
```

The trait is implemented for:

- `Result<T, E>` where `E: Into<anyhow::Error>` → wraps `Ok(t)` in `Output::Render(t)`
- `HandlerResult<T>` → passes through unchanged

This is used internally by `SimpleFnHandler` and the `#[handler]` macro.

---

## HandlerResult

`HandlerResult<T>` is a standard `Result` type:

```rust,ignore
pub type HandlerResult<T> = Result<Output<T>, anyhow::Error>;
```

The `?` operator works naturally for error propagation:

```rust,ignore
fn list_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Items> {
    let items = storage::load()?;           // Propagates errors
    let filtered = filter_items(&items)?;   // Propagates errors
    Ok(Output::Render(Items { filtered }))
}
```

### Authoritative external failures

When a handler delegates to another executable and the application's contract
requires that executable's exact nonzero status and stderr, return the public
`ExternalFailure` type through the same `HandlerResult` seam:

```rust,ignore
let failure = ExternalFailure::new(128, git_stderr)?;
Err(failure.into())
```

Construction rejects status `0`. Standout recognizes only this concrete type,
preserves its diagnostic verbatim, and exposes it as `RunErrorKind::External`.
Ordinary handler errors still use status `1`; this is not a general exit-code
mapping mechanism. Handlers must not print or call `process::exit` themselves.

---

## The Output Enum

`Output<T>` represents what a handler produces:

```rust,ignore
#[non_exhaustive]
pub enum Output<T: Serialize> {
    Render(T),
    Silent,
    Binary { data: Vec<u8>, filename: String },
    Artifact(Artifact<T>),
}
```

`Output` is `#[non_exhaustive]`: matches on it need a `_` arm so later shapes
can be added without breaking downstream code.

### Output::Render(T)

The common case. Data is passed to the render function:

```rust,ignore
#[derive(Serialize)]
struct ListResult {
    items: Vec<Item>,
    total: usize,
}

fn list_handler(_m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<ListResult> {
    let items = storage::list()?;
    Ok(Output::Render(ListResult {
        total: items.len(),
        items,
    }))
}
```

### Output::Silent

No output produced. Useful for commands with side effects only:

```rust,ignore
fn delete_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<()> {
    let id: &String = matches.get_one("id").unwrap();
    storage::delete(id)?;
    Ok(Output::Silent)
}
```

Silent behavior:

- Post-output hooks still receive `RenderedOutput::Silent`
- Render function is not called
- Nothing prints to stdout

### Output::Binary

Raw bytes for file output:

```rust,ignore
fn export_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<()> {
    let data = generate_report()?;
    let pdf_bytes = render_to_pdf(&data)?;

    Ok(Output::Binary {
        data: pdf_bytes,
        filename: "report.pdf".into(),
    })
}
```

Binary output bypasses the render function entirely.

The filename is a **hint for the caller**, not permission to write. Without
`--output-file-path`, `run()` sends the bytes to stdout and touches no file. If
you want the framework to write the suggested destination, use `Output::Artifact`
— that opt-in is the whole difference between the two shapes.

### Output::Artifact

Owned bytes plus an application-owned report, for commands that produce a file
*and* have something to say about it. `Output::Binary` cannot carry a report,
and nothing renders after its write, so a command that wants to say "exported 12
rows to /tmp/report.csv (2 warnings)" would otherwise have to write the file
itself — pulling destination policy back into the application core.

```rust,ignore
use standout::cli::{Artifact, HandlerResult, Output};

#[derive(Serialize)]
struct ExportReport {
    exported: usize,
    warnings: Vec<Warning>,
}

fn export_handler(_m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<ExportReport> {
    let export = core::export_csv()?;   // bytes + facts, no filesystem

    Ok(Output::Artifact(
        Artifact::new(export.csv)
            .suggest_destination(export.suggested_filename)
            .with_report(ExportReport {
                exported: export.rows,
                warnings: export.warnings,
            }),
    ))
}
```

Who owns what:

| Concern | Owner |
| --- | --- |
| Artifact bytes | Application |
| Suggested destination | Application (a suggestion) |
| Semantic report and warning taxonomy | Application |
| Destination selection | Framework |
| The write and its failure | Framework |
| Receipt (completed destination) | Framework |

#### Destination policy

Standout selects the destination deterministically:

1. the explicit `--output-file-path` override;
2. the artifact's `suggest_destination(...)`, if the application opted in;
3. stdout, if the application opted in with `allow_stdout()`.

If none applies, the run fails with `FinalWrite(Artifact)` rather than inventing
a file or dropping the bytes. All three steps share that one failure path.

#### Write first, report second

Standout writes, then renders the report from a fixed envelope:

```json
{
  "report": { "exported": 12, "warnings": [] },
  "receipt": { "destination": "/tmp/report.csv", "stdout": false, "byte_count": 480 }
}
```

So a template can say what only the framework knows:

```jinja
Exported {{ report.exported }} rows to {{ receipt.destination }}
```

The envelope shape is fixed (`report` + `receipt`) whatever the report's type,
so no application key can collide with the receipt. Structured modes serialize
the same envelope. A failed write renders nothing: success cannot outrun the
write that justifies it.

#### The report channel

Mixing a report into the bytes would corrupt them, so the channel follows the
destination:

| Artifact destination | Report goes to |
| --- | --- |
| File | stdout |
| Stdout (`allow_stdout()`) | stderr |

#### Hooks and artifacts

Post-dispatch hooks see the report as ordinary handler data. Post-output hooks
see `RenderedOutput::Artifact` and can still transform the bytes or the report
via `as_artifact_mut()`. Hooks never perform the write — that stays framework-
owned, which is what keeps the failure path single and the report honest.

Bytes are owned; streaming is deliberately not part of this contract.

---

## CommandContext

`CommandContext` provides execution environment information and state access:

```rust,ignore
pub struct CommandContext {
    pub command_path: Vec<String>,
    pub app_state: Rc<Extensions>,
    pub extensions: Extensions,
}
```

**command_path**: The subcommand chain as a vector, e.g., `["db", "migrate"]`. Useful for logging or conditional logic.

**app_state**: Shared, immutable state configured at app build time via `AppBuilder::app_state()`. Wrapped in `Arc` for cheap cloning. Use for database connections, configuration, API clients.

**extensions**: Per-request, mutable state injected by pre-dispatch hooks. Use for user sessions, request IDs, computed values.

> For comprehensive coverage of state management, see [App State and Extensions](app-state.md).

---

## State Access: App State vs Extensions

Handlers access state through two distinct mechanisms with different semantics:

| Aspect         | `ctx.app_state`               | `ctx.extensions`           |
| -------------- | ----------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| **Mutability** | Immutable (`&`)               | Mutable (`&mut`)           |
| **Lifetime**   | App lifetime                  | Per-request                |
| **Set by**     | `AppBuilder::app_state()`     | Pre-dispatch hooks         |
| **Use for**    | Database, Config, API clients | User sessions, request IDs |

### App State (Shared Resources)

Configure long-lived resources at build time:

```rust,ignore
App::builder()
    .app_state(Database::connect()?)
    .app_state(Config::load()?)
    .command("list", list_handler, template)?
    .build()?
```

Access in handlers via `ctx.app_state`:

```rust,ignore
fn list_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Vec<Item>> {
    let db = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?;
    let config = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Config>()?;

    let items = db.query_items(config.max_results)?;
    Ok(Output::Render(items))
}
```

### Extensions (Per-Request State)

Pre-dispatch hooks inject request-scoped state:

```rust,ignore
use standout_dispatch::{Hooks, HookError};

struct UserScope { user_id: String, permissions: Vec<String> }

let hooks = Hooks::new()
    .pre_dispatch(|matches, ctx| {
        // Can read app_state to set up per-request state
        let db = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?;

        let user_id = matches.get_one::<String>("user").unwrap().clone();
        let permissions = db.get_permissions(&user_id)?;

        ctx.extensions.insert(UserScope { user_id, permissions });
        Ok(())
    });
```

Handlers retrieve from extensions:

```rust,ignore
fn list_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Vec<Item>> {
    let db = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?;       // shared
    let scope = ctx.extensions.get_required::<UserScope>()?;  // per-request

    let items = db.list_for_user(&scope.user_id)?;
    Ok(Output::Render(items))
}
```

### Extensions API

Both `app_state` and `extensions` use the same `Extensions` type with these methods:

| Method              | Description                                     |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `insert<T>(value)`  | Insert a value, returns previous if any         |
| `get<T>()`          | Get immutable reference, returns `Option<&T>`   |
| `get_required<T>()` | Get reference or return error if missing        |
| `get_mut<T>()`      | Get mutable reference, returns `Option<&mut T>` |
| `remove<T>()`       | Remove and return value                         |
| `contains<T>()`     | Check if type exists                            |
| `len()`             | Number of stored values                         |
| `is_empty()`        | True if no values stored                        |
| `clear()`           | Remove all values                               |

Use `get_required` for mandatory dependencies (fails fast with clear error), `get` for optional ones.

### When to Use Which

**Use App State for:**

- Database connections — expensive to create, should be pooled
- Configuration — loaded once at startup
- API clients — shared HTTP clients with connection pooling

**Use Extensions for:**

- User context — current user, session, permissions
- Request metadata — request ID, timing, correlation ID
- Transient state — data computed by one hook, used by handler

### The Two-State Pattern

The separation exists because:

1. **Closure capture doesn't work with `#[derive(Dispatch)]`** — macro-generated dispatch calls handlers with a fixed signature
2. **App-level resources shouldn't be created per-request** — database pools and config are expensive
3. **Per-request state needs mutable injection** — hooks compute values at runtime

```rust,ignore
// App state: configured once at build time
App::builder()
    .app_state(Database::connect()?)  // Shared via Arc
    .hooks("users.list", Hooks::new()
        .pre_dispatch(|matches, ctx| {
            // Extensions: computed per-request, can use app_state
            let db = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?;
            let user = authenticate(matches, db)?;
            ctx.extensions.insert(user);
            Ok(())
        }))?
```

> For comprehensive coverage of state management patterns, see [App State and Extensions](app-state.md).

---

## Accessing CLI Arguments

The `ArgMatches` parameter provides access to parsed arguments through clap's standard API:

```rust,ignore
fn handler(matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Data> {
    // Flags
    let verbose = matches.get_flag("verbose");

    // Required options
    let name: &String = matches.get_one("name").unwrap();

    // Optional values
    let limit: Option<&u32> = matches.get_one("limit");

    // Multiple values
    let tags: Vec<&String> = matches.get_many("tags")
        .map(|v| v.collect())
        .unwrap_or_default();

    Ok(Output::Render(Data { ... }))
}
```

For subcommands, you work with the `ArgMatches` for your specific command level.

---

## Testing Handlers

Because handlers have explicit inputs and outputs, their adapter behavior is
straightforward to test directly. Test validation, filtering, and state
transitions through the CLI-free library instead:

```rust,ignore
#[test]
fn test_list_handler() {
    let cmd = Command::new("test")
        .arg(Arg::new("verbose").long("verbose").action(ArgAction::SetTrue));
    let matches = cmd.try_get_matches_from(["test", "--verbose"]).unwrap();

    let ctx = CommandContext {
        command_path: vec!["list".into()],
        ..Default::default()
    };

    let result = list_handler(&matches, &ctx);

    assert!(result.is_ok());
    if let Ok(Output::Render(data)) = result {
        assert!(data.verbose);
    }
}
```

No mocking frameworks needed—construct `ArgMatches` with clap, create a `CommandContext`, call your handler, assert on the result.

### Testing with App State

When handlers depend on app_state, inject test fixtures:

```rust,ignore
#[test]
fn test_handler_with_app_state() {
    use std::sync::Arc;

    // Create test fixtures
    let mock_db = MockDatabase::with_items(vec![
        Item { id: "1", name: "Test" }
    ]);

    // Build app_state with test data
    let mut app_state = Extensions::new();
    app_state.insert(mock_db);

    let ctx = CommandContext {
        command_path: vec!["list".into()],
        app_state: Arc::new(app_state),
        extensions: Extensions::new(),
    };

    let cmd = Command::new("test");
    let matches = cmd.try_get_matches_from(["test"]).unwrap();

    let result = list_handler(&matches, &ctx);
    assert!(result.is_ok());
}
```

### Testing Handlers with Mutable State

Handler tests can verify state mutation across calls:

```rust,ignore
#[test]
fn test_handler_state_mutation() {
    struct Counter { count: u32 }

    impl Handler for Counter {
        type Output = u32;
        fn handle(&mut self, _m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<u32> {
            self.count += 1;
            Ok(Output::Render(self.count))
        }
    }

    let mut handler = Counter { count: 0 };
    let cmd = Command::new("test");
    let matches = cmd.try_get_matches_from(["test"]).unwrap();
    let ctx = CommandContext {
        command_path: vec!["count".into()],
        ..Default::default()
    };

    // State accumulates across calls
    let _ = handler.handle(&matches, &ctx);
    let _ = handler.handle(&matches, &ctx);
    let result = handler.handle(&matches, &ctx);

    assert!(matches!(result, Ok(Output::Render(3))));
}
```

1	# List Views
2	
3	Most CLI commands that print a collection share the same shape: an optional
4	intro line, the items, an optional list of messages (warnings, info), and an
5	optional summary of how many items were filtered out of a larger total. The
6	`list_view` builder in `standout::views` captures that shape once so handlers
7	stop reassembling it by hand, and `#[dispatch(list_view)]` wires the result to
8	the framework's built-in list template without a project-owned template file.
9	
10	Reach for it whenever a handler returns "here are N things" — a `list`,
11	`search`, or `status` command — and the result needs more than a bare `Vec<T>`:
12	an intro line, a filter summary, or per-item messages.
13	
14	## Where it lives
15	
16	`list_view`, `ListViewBuilder`, and `ListViewResult` live in
17	`standout::views`, a module (`pub mod views`) rather than a crate-root
18	re-export:
19	
20	```rust
21	use standout::views::{list_view, ListViewBuilder, ListViewResult};
22	```
23	
24	## The builder
25	
26	```rust
27	pub fn list_view<T>(items: impl IntoIterator<Item = T>) -> ListViewBuilder<T>;
28	```
29	
30	`ListViewBuilder<T>` accepts items in any order and returns itself, so calls
31	chain:
32	
33	| Method | Effect |
34	| --- | --- |
35	| `.intro(text)` | A line shown before the items |
36	| `.ending(text)` | A line shown after the items |
37	| `.message(level, text)` | Attaches a `Message` at the given `MessageLevel` |
38	| `.info(text)` | Shortcut for `.message(MessageLevel::Info, text)` |
39	| `.success(text)` | Shortcut for `.message(MessageLevel::Success, text)` |
40	| `.warning(text)` | Shortcut for `.message(MessageLevel::Warning, text)` |
41	| `.error(text)` | Shortcut for `.message(MessageLevel::Error, text)` |
42	| `.total_count(n)` | Records the unfiltered total, for a "showing X of Y" summary |
43	| `.filter_summary(text)` | A human-readable description of the active filter |
44	| `.tabular_spec(spec)` | Attaches a `TabularSpec` directly (usually left to `#[dispatch(list_view, item_type = "...")]` instead) |
45	| `.build()` | Consumes the builder and returns a `ListViewResult<T>` |
46	
47	## The result
48	
49	```rust
50	pub struct ListViewResult<T> {
51	    pub items: Vec<T>,
52	    pub intro: Option<String>,
53	    pub ending: Option<String>,
54	    pub messages: Vec<Message>,
55	    pub total_count: Option<usize>,
56	    pub filter_summary: Option<String>,
57	    pub tabular_spec: Option<TabularSpec>,
58	}
59	```
60	
61	`ListViewResult<T>` implements `Serialize` (fields that are `None` or empty
62	are skipped, so `--output json` stays uncluttered), `Default` (an empty list
63	with every optional field unset), and carries `.is_empty()` and `.len()`
64	methods that read `items` directly.
65	
66	Because it derives `Serialize` rather than requiring one, `ListViewResult<T>`
67	is itself a valid handler return type: a handler can return
68	`HandlerResult<ListViewResult<Task>>` and wrap it in `Output::Render` like any
69	other structured output. See
70	[Handler Contract](../crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md) for the
71	`Output` enum and the render pipeline it feeds.

73	## Connecting to `#[dispatch(list_view)]`
74

# List Views

Most CLI commands that print a collection share the same shape: an optional
intro line, the items, an optional list of messages (warnings, info), and an
optional summary of how many items were filtered out of a larger total. The
`list_view` builder in `standout::views` captures that shape once so handlers
stop reassembling it by hand, and `#[dispatch(list_view)]` wires the result to
the framework's built-in list template without a project-owned template file.

Reach for it whenever a handler returns "here are N things" — a `list`,
`search`, or `status` command — and the result needs more than a bare `Vec<T>`:
an intro line, a filter summary, or per-item messages.

## Where it lives

`list_view`, `ListViewBuilder`, and `ListViewResult` live in
`standout::views`, a module (`pub mod views`) rather than a crate-root
re-export:

```rust
use standout::views::{list_view, ListViewBuilder, ListViewResult};
```

## The builder

```rust
pub fn list_view<T>(items: impl IntoIterator<Item = T>) -> ListViewBuilder<T>;
```

`ListViewBuilder<T>` accepts items in any order and returns itself, so calls
chain:

| Method | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `.intro(text)` | A line shown before the items |
| `.ending(text)` | A line shown after the items |
| `.message(level, text)` | Attaches a `Message` at the given `MessageLevel` |
| `.info(text)` | Shortcut for `.message(MessageLevel::Info, text)` |
| `.success(text)` | Shortcut for `.message(MessageLevel::Success, text)` |
| `.warning(text)` | Shortcut for `.message(MessageLevel::Warning, text)` |
| `.error(text)` | Shortcut for `.message(MessageLevel::Error, text)` |
| `.total_count(n)` | Records the unfiltered total, for a "showing X of Y" summary |
| `.filter_summary(text)` | A human-readable description of the active filter |
| `.tabular_spec(spec)` | Attaches a `TabularSpec` directly (usually left to `#[dispatch(list_view, item_type = "...")]` instead) |
| `.build()` | Consumes the builder and returns a `ListViewResult<T>` |

## The result

```rust
pub struct ListViewResult<T> {
    pub items: Vec<T>,
    pub intro: Option<String>,
    pub ending: Option<String>,
    pub messages: Vec<Message>,
    pub total_count: Option<usize>,
    pub filter_summary: Option<String>,
    pub tabular_spec: Option<TabularSpec>,
}
```

`ListViewResult<T>` implements `Serialize` (fields that are `None` or empty
are skipped, so `--output json` stays uncluttered), `Default` (an empty list
with every optional field unset), and carries `.is_empty()` and `.len()`
methods that read `items` directly.

Because it derives `Serialize` rather than requiring one, `ListViewResult<T>`
is itself a valid handler return type: a handler can return
`HandlerResult<ListViewResult<Task>>` and wrap it in `Output::Render` like any
other structured output. See
[Handler Contract](../crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md) for the
`Output` enum and the render pipeline it feeds.

## Connecting to `#[dispatch(list_view)]`

The `Dispatch` derive has a `list_view` variant attribute that does two
things to a variant's handler:

- It sets the command's template to the framework-provided
  `standout/list-view` template, unless the variant also sets
  `#[dispatch(template_name = "...")]`, in which case that name wins.
- If `item_type = "..."` names a type implementing `Tabular`, the derive
  wraps the handler so that, on a successful `Output::Render(list_view_result)`,
  it stamps `list_view_result.tabular_spec` with `<ItemType as Tabular>::tabular_spec()`
  before rendering. The handler itself never has to know about the column
  layout.

Handlers under `#[dispatch(list_view)]` can be either the two-argument shape
(`fn(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<ListViewResult<T>>`) or,
with `#[dispatch(simple)]` added, a single-argument shape
(`fn(&ArgMatches) -> HandlerResult<ListViewResult<T>>`). Both are wrapped the
same way.

## Worked example

```rust
use clap::{ArgMatches, Subcommand};
use serde::Serialize;
use standout::cli::{CommandContext, Dispatch, HandlerResult, Output};
use standout::views::list_view;
use standout::{Tabular, TabularRow};

#[derive(Serialize, Tabular, TabularRow, Clone)]
struct Task {
    #[col(width = 5)]
    id: u32,
    #[col(width = 20)]
    name: String,
}

mod handlers {
    use super::*;

    pub fn list(
        _matches: &ArgMatches,
        _ctx: &CommandContext,
    ) -> HandlerResult<standout::views::ListViewResult<Task>> {
        let tasks = vec![Task {
            id: 1,
            name: "Write docs".to_string(),
        }];
        Ok(Output::Render(list_view(tasks).build()))
    }
}

#[derive(Subcommand, Dispatch)]
#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
enum Commands {
    #[dispatch(list_view, item_type = "Task")]
    List,
}
```

Running `list` renders the framework's list template with `Task`'s column
widths already attached; `--output json` serializes the same
`ListViewResult<Task>`, `tabular_spec` included, with no template involved.
An empty `items` vec renders the template's "No items found" branch rather
than an empty table.

## Disabling the framework template

`App::builder().include_framework_templates(false)` refuses to build if a
command names `standout/list-view` (or any other framework template) without
supplying a replacement — a project can opt out of the built-in list layout,
but only by registering its own template under the same name.
