1	# Templating
2	
3	`standout-render` uses a two-pass templating system that combines a template engine for logic and data binding with a custom BBCode-like syntax for styling. This separation keeps templates readable while providing full control over both content and presentation.
4	
5	The default engine is MiniJinja (Jinja2-compatible), but alternative engines are available. See [Template Engines](template-engines.md) for options including a lightweight `SimpleEngine` for reduced binary size.
6	
7	---
8	
9	## Two-Pass Rendering Pipeline
10	
11	Templates are processed in two distinct passes:
12	
13	```text
14	Template + Data → [Pass 1: MiniJinja] → Text with style tags → [Pass 2: BBParser] → Final output
15	```
16	
17	**Pass 1 - MiniJinja**: Standard template processing. Variables are substituted, control flow executes, filters apply.
18	
19	**Pass 2 - BBParser**: Style tag processing. Bracket-notation tags are converted to ANSI escape codes (or stripped, depending on output mode).
20	
21	### Pipeline Example
22	
23	```text
24	Template:     [title]{{ name }}[/title] has {{ count }} items
25	Data:         { name: "Report", count: 42 }
26	
27	After Pass 1: [title]Report[/title] has 42 items
28	After Pass 2: \x1b[1;36mReport\x1b[0m has 42 items  (or plain: "Report has 42 items")
29	```
30	
31	This separation means:
32	
33	- Template logic (loops, conditionals) is handled by MiniJinja—a mature, well-documented engine
34	- Style application is a simple, predictable transformation
35	- You can debug each pass independently
36	
37	---
38	
39	## MiniJinja Basics
40	
41	MiniJinja implements Jinja2 syntax, a widely-used templating language. Here's a quick overview:
42	
43	### Variables
44	
45	```jinja
46	{{ variable }}
47	{{ object.field }}
48	{{ list[0] }}
49	```
50	
51	### Control Flow
52	
53	```jinja
54	{% if condition %}
55	  Show this
56	{% elif other_condition %}
57	  Show that
58	{% else %}
59	  Default
60	{% endif %}
61	
62	{% for item in items %}
63	  {{ loop.index }}. {{ item.name }}
64	{% endfor %}
65	```
66	
67	### Filters
68	
69	```jinja
70	{{ name | upper }}
71	{{ list | length }}
72	{{ value | default("N/A") }}
73	{{ text | truncate(20) }}
74	```
75	
76	### Comments
77	
78	```jinja
79	{# This is a comment and won't appear in output #}
80	```
81	
82	For comprehensive MiniJinja documentation, see the [MiniJinja documentation](https://docs.rs/minijinja).
83	
84	### Booleans and None
85	
86	Standout renders these the Rust way — `true`, `false`, `none` — not the Jinja2
87	way MiniJinja itself uses (`True`, `False`, `None`). This holds for
88	interpolation, loop and `set` bindings, `| string`, `| join`, sequence and map
89	literals, standout's own filters, and table cells:
90	
91	```jinja
92	{{ flag }}                {# true #}
93	{{ missing }}             {# none #}
94	{{ flags }}               {# [true, false, none] #}
95	{{ flags | join(", ") }}  {# true, false, none #}
96	```
97	
98	Two exceptions:
99	
100	- The `~` concatenation operator formats inside MiniJinja's evaluator, which
101	  exposes no hook: `{{ "x" ~ flag }}` yields `xTrue`. Write `{{ "x" }}{{ flag }}`
102	  or `{{ "x" ~ flag | string }}`.
103	- Structured output (JSON, YAML, XML, CSV) skips templates entirely and
104	  serializes your data directly, so those modes follow their format's own rules.
105	
106	If you build a `minijinja::Environment` yourself, use
107	`standout_render::template::new_environment()` — or call `register_filters` on
108	your own environment, which installs the same spelling.
109	
110	---
111	
112	## The Trailing-Newline Contract
113	
114	Two things happen to the newline at the end of a template, and together they
115	are observable in the bytes a script reads, so they are stated here rather than
116	discovered by probing.
117	
118	**The engine consumes exactly one final newline.** This is Jinja's rule and
119	MiniJinja keeps it. A template file ending in a single `\n` renders with no
120	trailing newline at all; a file ending in two renders with one.
121	
122	| Template source | Rendered string |
123	| --- | --- |
124	| `{{ name }}` | `x` |
125	| `{{ name }}\n` | `x` |
126	| `{{ name }}\n\n` | `x\n` |
127	| `{{ name }}\n\n\n` | `x\n\n` |
128	
129	**The process edge appends exactly one newline.** `App::run` writes a handled
130	command's text with `writeln!`, so what reaches stdout is the rendered string
131	plus one `\n` — whatever the template ended with.
132	
133	The practical consequence: a template that ends with one newline and a template
134	that ends with none produce identical bytes. To end a page with a blank line,
135	the template needs *two* trailing newlines. Every editor that adds a final
136	newline on save is therefore invisible here, which is the reason the rule is
137	worth stating.
138	
139	`standout-render/tests/trailing_newline.rs` pins the engine half;
140	`final_emission_routes_success_and_diagnostics_to_distinct_streams` in
141	`standout/src/cli/builder/execution.rs` pins the process half.
142	
143	---
144	
145	## Style Tags
146	
147	Style tags use BBCode-like bracket notation to apply named styles from your theme:
148	
149	```jinja
150	[style-name]content to style[/style-name]
151	```
152	
153	### Basic Usage
154	
155	```jinja
156	[title]Report Summary[/title]
157	[error]Something went wrong![/error]
158	[muted]Last updated: {{ timestamp }}[/muted]
159	```
160	
161	### Nesting
162	
163	Tags can nest properly:
164	
165	```jinja
166	[outer][inner]nested content[/inner][/outer]
167	```
168	
169	### Spanning Lines
170	
171	Tags can span multiple lines:
172	
173	```jinja
174	[panel]
175	This is a multi-line
176	block of styled content
177	[/panel]
178	```
179	
180	### With Template Logic
181	
182	Style tags and MiniJinja work together seamlessly:
183	
184	```jinja
185	[title]{% if custom_title %}{{ custom_title }}{% else %}Default Title{% endif %}[/title]
186	
187	{% for task in tasks %}
188	[{{ task.status }}]{{ task.title }}[/{{ task.status }}]
189	{% endfor %}
190	```
191	
192	The second example shows dynamic style names—the style applied depends on the value of `task.status`.
193	
194	---
195	
196	## Processing Modes
197	
198	Pass 2 (BBParser) processes style tags differently based on the output mode:
199	
200	| Mode | Behavior | Use Case |
201	| ------ | ---------- | ---------- |
202	| `Term` | Replace tags with ANSI escape codes | Rich terminal output |
203	| `Text` | Strip tags completely | Plain text, pipes, files |
204	| `TermDebug` | Keep tags as literal text | Debugging, testing |
205	
206	### Processing Modes Example
207	
208	Template: `[title]Hello[/title]`
209	
210	- **Term**: `\x1b[1;36mHello\x1b[0m` (rendered as cyan bold)
211	- **Text**: `Hello`
212	- **TermDebug**: `[title]Hello[/title]`
213	
214	### Setting the Mode
215	
216	```rust
217	use standout_render::{render_with_output, OutputMode};
218	
219	// Rich terminal
220	let output = render_with_output(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Term)?;
221	
222	// Plain text
223	let output = render_with_output(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Text)?;
224	
225	// Debug (tags visible)
226	let output = render_with_output(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::TermDebug)?;
227	
228	// Auto-detect based on TTY
229	let output = render_with_output(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Auto)?;
230	```
231	
232	### Auto Mode
233	
234	`OutputMode::Auto` detects the appropriate mode:
235	
236	- If stdout is a TTY with color support → `Term`
237	- If stdout is a pipe or redirect → `Text`
238	
239	> **For standout framework users:** The framework's `--output` CLI flag automatically sets the output mode. See standout documentation for details.
240	
241	---
242	
243	## Built-in Filters
244	
245	Beyond MiniJinja's standard filters, `standout-render` provides formatting filters:
246	
247	### Column Formatting
248	
249	```jinja
250	{{ value | col(10) }}                              {# pad/truncate to 10 chars #}
251	{{ value | col(20, align="right") }}               {# right-align in 20 chars #}
252	{{ value | col(15, truncate="middle") }}           {# truncate in middle #}
253	{{ value | col(15, truncate="start", ellipsis="...") }}
254	```
255	
256	### Padding
257	
258	```jinja
259	{{ "42" | pad_left(8) }}      {# "      42" #}
260	{{ "hi" | pad_right(8) }}     {# "hi      " #}
261	{{ "hi" | pad_center(8) }}    {# "   hi   " #}
262	```
263	
264	### Truncation
265	
266	```jinja
267	{{ long_text | truncate_at(20) }}                   {# "Very long text th..." #}
268	{{ path | truncate_at(30, "middle", "...") }}      {# "/home/.../file.txt" #}
269	{{ text | truncate_at(20, "start") }}              {# "...end of the text" #}
270	```
271	
272	### Display Width
273	
274	```jinja
275	{% if value | display_width > 20 %}
276	  {{ value | truncate_at(20) }}
277	{% else %}
278	  {{ value }}
279	{% endif %}
280	```
281	
282	Returns visual width (handles Unicode—CJK characters count as 2).
283	
284	### Style Application
285	
286	```jinja
287	{{ value | style_as("error") }}                    {# wraps in [error]...[/error] #}
288	{{ task.status | style_as(task.status) }}         {# dynamic: [pending]pending[/pending] #}
289	```
290	
291	---
292	
293	## Template Registry
294	
295	When using the `Renderer` struct, templates are resolved by name through a registry:
296	
297	```rust
298	use standout_render::Renderer;
299	
300	let mut renderer = Renderer::new(theme)?;
301	
302	// Add inline template
303	renderer.add_template("greeting", "Hello, [name]{{ name }}[/name]!")?;
304	
305	// Add directory of templates
306	renderer.add_template_dir("./templates")?;
307	
308	// Render by name
309	let output = renderer.render("greeting", &data)?;
310	```
311	
312	### Resolution Priority
313	
314	1. **Inline templates** (added via `add_template()`)
315	2. **Directory templates** (from `add_template_dir()`)
316	
317	### File Extensions
318	
319	Supported extensions (in priority order): `.jinja`, `.jinja2`, `.j2`, `.stpl`, `.txt`
320	
321	When you request `"report"`, the registry checks:
322	
323	- Inline template named `"report"`
324	- `report.jinja` in registered directories
325	- `report.jinja2`, `report.j2`, `report.stpl`, `report.txt` (lower priority)
326	
327	The `.stpl` extension is for SimpleEngine templates. See [Template Engines](template-engines.md) for details.
328	
329	### Template Names
330	
331	Template names are derived from relative paths:
332	
333	```text
334	templates/
335	├── greeting.jinja       → "greeting"
336	├── reports/
337	│   └── summary.jinja    → "reports/summary"
338	└── errors/
339	    └── 404.jinja        → "errors/404"
340	```
341	
342	---
343	
344	## Including Templates
345	
346	Templates can include other templates using MiniJinja's include syntax:
347	
348	```jinja
349	{# main.jinja #}
350	[title]{{ title }}[/title]
351	
352	{% include "partials/header.jinja" %}
353	
354	{% for item in items %}
355	  {% include "partials/item.jinja" %}
356	{% endfor %}
357	
358	{% include "partials/footer.jinja" %}
359	```
360	
361	This enables reusable components across your application.
362	
363	---
364	
365	## Context Variables
366	
367	Beyond your data, you can inject additional context into templates:
368	
369	```rust
370	use standout_render::{render_with_vars, OutputMode};
371	use std::collections::HashMap;
372	
373	let mut vars = HashMap::new();
374	vars.insert("version", "1.0.0");
375	vars.insert("app_name", "MyApp");
376	
377	let output = render_with_vars(
378	    "{{ app_name }} v{{ version }}: {{ message }}",
379	    &data,
380	    &theme,
381	    OutputMode::Term,
382	    vars,
383	)?;
384	```
385	
386	When handler data and context variables have the same key, **handler data wins**. Context is supplementary.
387	
388	---
389	
390	## Structured Output
391	
392	For machine-readable output (JSON, YAML, CSV), templates are bypassed entirely:
393	
394	```rust
395	use standout_render::{render_auto, OutputMode};
396	
397	// Template is used for Term/Text modes
398	// Data is serialized directly for Json/Yaml/Csv
399	let output = render_auto(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Json)?;
400	```
401	
402	| Mode | Behavior |
403	| ------ | ---------- |
404	| `Term` | Render template, apply styles |
405	| `Text` | Render template, strip styles |
406	| `TermDebug` | Render template, keep style tags |
407	| `Json` | `serde_json::to_string_pretty(data)` |
408	| `Yaml` | `serde_yaml::to_string(data)` |
409	| `Csv` | Flatten and format as CSV |
410	
411	This means your serializable data types automatically support structured output without additional code.
412	
413	---
414	
415	## Validation
416	
417	Check templates for unknown style tags before deploying:
418	
419	```rust
420	use standout_render::validate_template;
421	
422	let errors = validate_template(template, &sample_data, &theme);
423	if !errors.is_empty() {
424	    for error in &errors {
425	        eprintln!("Unknown style tag: [{}]", error.tag_name);
426	    }
427	}
428	```
429	
430	Validation catches:
431	
432	- Misspelled style names
433	- References to undefined styles
434	- Mismatched opening/closing tags
435	
436	---
437	
438	## API Reference
439	
440	### Render Functions
441	
442	```rust
443	use standout_render::{
444	    render,                  // Basic: template + data + theme
445	    render_with_output,      // With explicit output mode
446	    render_with_mode,        // With output mode + color mode
447	    render_with_vars,        // With extra context variables
448	    render_auto,             // Auto-dispatch template vs serialize
449	    render_auto_with_context,
450	};
451	
452	// Basic
453	let output = render(template, &data, &theme)?;
454	
455	// With output mode
456	let output = render_with_output(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Term)?;
457	
458	// With color mode override (for testing)
459	let output = render_with_mode(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Term, ColorMode::Dark)?;
460	
461	// Auto (template for text modes, serialize for structured)
462	let output = render_auto(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Json)?;
463	```
464	
465	### Renderer Struct
466	
467	```rust
468	use standout_render::Renderer;
469	
470	let mut renderer = Renderer::new(theme)?;
471	renderer.add_template("name", "content")?;
472	renderer.add_template_dir("./templates")?;
473	
474	let output = renderer.render("name", &data)?;
475	let output = renderer.render_with_mode("name", &data, OutputMode::Text)?;
476	```
477

# Production-shaped application

When an application has behavior worth reusing or testing independently, keep
that behavior in a fully CLI-free library and put every shell concern in the
binary package.

The repository's canonical [`tdoo` worked example](../../crates/todo-example/README.md)
is executable documentation for that layout:

```text
todo-core (library)              tdoo (binary)
------------------------------   ---------------------------------
model and invariants             Clap commands and flags
validation and filtering         Standout App construction
state transitions                handlers as adapters
JSON persistence                 CLI view models
explicit storage path            env lookup, templates, styles
fast core tests                  hooks and TestHarness tests
```

The dependency arrow goes one way:

```text
tdoo  --->  todo-core
```

`todo-core` has no dependency on Clap, Standout, command contexts, environment
variables, view DTOs, templates, styles, or terminal output. Its interface is
the surface used by both the CLI and core tests.

The CLI translates at the seam. A handler maps `--all` to a core `TodoFilter`,
calls the store, then maps domain values to CLI-owned `TodoView` values. That
keeps structured output stable even when the library's persisted model changes.

Read the canonical source rather than copying a second implementation here:

- [`todo-core/src/lib.rs`](../../crates/todo-example/todo-core/src/lib.rs) — the
  small public library interface;
- [`todo-core/src/store.rs`](../../crates/todo-example/todo-core/src/store.rs) —
  behavior, persistence, and fast tests;
- [`tdoo/src/handlers.rs`](../../crates/todo-example/tdoo/src/handlers.rs) — thin
  adapters and direct typed-handler tests;
- [`tdoo/src/app.rs`](../../crates/todo-example/tdoo/src/app.rs) — app assembly,
  shell pipeline features, and focused `TestHarness` tests.

For a five-minute look at dispatch and rendering without the package split, use
the [minimal single-crate example](minimal-single-crate.md).

For a broader review of ownership, rendering, testing, and optional framework
capabilities, use the
[Leveraging Standout implementation quality checklist](leveraging-standout.md).

1	# Minimal single-crate example
2	
3	This self-contained project is a compact way to see Standout's dispatch and
4	rendering pipeline. It keeps everything in one binary package for brevity; it
5	is not the recommended layout for an application with reusable logic.
6	
7	For production-shaped ownership, continue to the
8	[two-package worked application](production-shaped-example.md), where a
9	CLI-free library owns application behavior and a binary owns all CLI concerns.
10	
11	## File structure
12	
13	```text
14	my-todo/
15	├── Cargo.toml
16	└── src/
17	    ├── main.rs
18	    ├── templates/list.jinja
19	    └── styles/default.css
20	```
21	
22	## Cargo.toml
23	
24	```toml
25	[package]
26	name = "my-todo"
27	version = "0.1.0"
28	edition = "2021"
29	
30	[dependencies]
31	standout = "9"
32	clap = { version = "4", features = ["derive"] }
33	serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
34	anyhow = "1"
35	```
36	
37	## `src/main.rs`
38	
39	```rust
40	use clap::{CommandFactory, Parser, Subcommand};
41	use serde::Serialize;
42	use standout::cli::{App, CommandContext, Dispatch, Output};
43	use standout::{embed_styles, embed_templates, handler};
44	
45	#[derive(Parser)]
46	#[command(name = "my-todo")]
47	struct Cli {
48	    #[command(subcommand)]
49	    command: Option<Commands>,
50	}
51	
52	#[derive(Subcommand, Dispatch)]
53	#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
54	enum Commands {
55	    /// List all todos. Running the binary with no command lists too.
56	    #[dispatch(pure, default)]
57	    List,
58	}
59	
60	#[derive(Serialize)]
61	struct TodoResult {
62	    todos: Vec<TodoView>,
63	}
64	
65	#[derive(Serialize)]
66	struct TodoView {
67	    title: String,
68	    status: String,
69	}
70	
71	mod handlers {
72	    use super::*;
73	
74	    // This is a CLI adapter returning view data. In a real application it
75	    // should call a CLI-free library rather than contain application behavior.
76	    #[handler]
77	    pub fn list(
78	        #[ctx] _ctx: &CommandContext,
79	    ) -> Result<Output<TodoResult>, anyhow::Error> {
80	        Ok(Output::Render(TodoResult {
81	            todos: vec![
82	                TodoView { title: "Write documentation".into(), status: "done".into() },
83	                TodoView { title: "Ship v1.0".into(), status: "pending".into() },
84	            ],
85	        }))
86	    }
87	}
88	
89	fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
90	    let app = App::builder()
91	        .version(env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION"))
92	        .templates(embed_templates!("src/templates"))
93	        .styles(embed_styles!("src/styles"))
94	        .default_theme("default")
95	        .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())?
96	        .build()?;
97	
98	    app.run(Cli::command(), std::env::args());
99	    Ok(())
100	}
101	```
102	
103	## `src/templates/list.jinja`
104	
105	```jinja
106	[title]My Todos[/title]
107	{% for todo in todos %}
108	[index]{{ loop.index }}.[/index] [{{ todo.status }}]{{ todo.title }}[/{{ todo.status }}]
109	{% endfor %}
110	```
111	
112	## `src/styles/default.css`
113	
114	```css
115	.title { color: cyan; font-weight: bold; }
116	.index { color: yellow; }
117	.done { color: gray; text-decoration: line-through; }
118	.pending { color: white; font-weight: bold; }
119	
120	@media (prefers-color-scheme: light) {
121	    .pending { color: black; }
122	}
123	```
124	
125	## Run it
126	
127	```bash
128	cargo run
129	cargo run -- list
130	cargo run -- list --output json
131	cargo run -- list --output text
132	```
133	
134	This demonstrates command dispatch, template rendering, structured output, hot
135	reload in debug builds, adaptive styles, and standout's themed `--help`, which
136	is on unless an application calls `.help_handling(false)`. It intentionally
137	does not teach package ownership or the testing pyramid; the
138	[production-shaped example](production-shaped-example.md) does.
139

1	# Passthrough Commands
2	
3	Every other way of registering a command — the `Dispatch` derive,
4	`command_with`, a `#[handler]` function — assumes the handler hands back
5	something serializable that Standout can render or serialize. A passthrough
6	command is the one registration shape without that assumption: the handler
7	writes its own bytes and returns `Result<(), anyhow::Error>`. ADR-0032 keeps
8	it as a secondary path for that reason: nothing else on the registration axis
9	accepts a signature with no serializable output and no render.
10	
11	Reach for it when a command's job is genuinely "run this external process and
12	let it own the terminal" — streaming a subprocess's output live, driving an
13	interactive prompt library that writes ANSI itself, or wrapping a tool that
14	already produces its own formatted output — not for handlers that happen to
15	print instead of returning data.
16	
17	## API
18	
19	```rust
20	impl AppBuilder {
21	    pub fn command_passthrough<F>(self, path: &str, handler: F) -> Result<Self, SetupError>
22	    where
23	        F: FnMut(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext) -> Result<(), anyhow::Error> + 'static;
24	}
25	```
26	
27	For a command declared inside `.commands(|g| ...)`, `GroupBuilder` has the
28	matching entry point:
29	
30	```rust
31	impl GroupBuilder {
32	    pub fn passthrough<F>(self, name: &str, handler: F) -> Self
33	    where
34	        F: FnMut(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext) -> Result<(), anyhow::Error> + 'static;
35	}
36	```
37	
38	Both take the same closure shape and register the command with no template:
39	there is nothing for a template to render.
40	
41	## What it does not get
42	
43	A passthrough command has no `Output` enum to return, so it gets none of the
44	things that come from having one:
45	
46	- No template. The command is registered with its template reference set to
47	  "absent, silently" — there is no configured or conventional template to
48	  resolve, by design, not by omission.
49	- No render pass, so no theme, no style tags, no `Tabular` columns.
50	- No structured output modes. `Output::Render` is what `--output json` (and
51	  `yaml`/`xml`/`csv`) serializes; a passthrough handler never produces an
52	  `Output` value, so those modes have nothing to act on.
53	- No post-dispatch hooks. The passthrough dispatch closure is handed the
54	  command's `Hooks` and ignores them, so nothing runs between the handler
55	  returning and the empty result leaving dispatch.
56	
57	App-level hooks registered for the command's path *do* still run, because they
58	sit outside the dispatch closure: a pre-dispatch hook runs before the handler
59	as it would for any command, and a post-output hook runs after it, receiving
60	`RenderedOutput::Silent`. A post-output hook attached to a passthrough command
61	is therefore not inert — it observes and can act, it just has no rendered text
62	to transform.
63	
64	Concretely, under `--output json` (or any other output mode) a passthrough
65	command runs exactly the same as under the default: the dispatch closure
66	backing `command_passthrough`/`passthrough` takes the output mode as a
67	parameter and ignores it. Standout's own output-writing pipeline resolves the
68	command to an empty string every time — whatever the handler wrote, it wrote
69	directly (to stdout, stderr, a file, wherever), outside that pipeline, and
70	`--output` has no way to reach it.
71	
72	## What the handler is responsible for
73	
74	Because nothing downstream will format or emit anything on the handler's
75	behalf, the handler owns:
76	
77	- Writing everything it wants seen — to stdout, stderr, or elsewhere.
78	- Its own error reporting for anything it prints before returning `Err(...)`;
79	  the `anyhow::Error` becomes the command's failure, but text already written
80	  stays written.
81	- Respecting (or explicitly ignoring) the user's terminal — colors, width,
82	  paging — since none of the framework's rendering machinery runs.
83	
84	## Worked example
85	
86	```rust
87	use anyhow::Context;
88	use clap::ArgMatches;
89	use standout::cli::{App, CommandContext};
90	use std::process::Command;
91	
92	fn run_migrations(_matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> Result<(), anyhow::Error> {
93	    let status = Command::new("./migrate.sh")
94	        .status()
95	        .context("failed to launch migrate.sh")?;
96	    if !status.success() {
97	        anyhow::bail!("migrate.sh exited with {status}");
98	    }
99	    Ok(())
100	}
101	
102	let app = App::builder()
103	    .command_passthrough("migrate", run_migrations)?
104	    .build()?;
105	```
106	
107	`migrate.sh`'s own stdout and stderr reach the terminal unchanged; Standout
108	neither captures nor reformats them.
109	
110	## When not to use it
111	
112	The blessed path is a `#[handler]` function returning `Result<T, E>`, wrapped
113	in `Output::Render` and rendered through a template — see
114	[Handler Contract](../crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md). Reach for
115	that whenever the command has any data a caller might want as JSON, any
116	output a template could format, or any reason to support `--output`. Use
117	passthrough only when the handler's whole job is to hand control to
118	something else that already owns its own bytes.
119

# Passthrough Commands

Every other way of registering a command — the `Dispatch` derive,
`command_with`, a `#[handler]` function — assumes the handler hands back
something serializable that Standout can render or serialize. A passthrough
command is the one registration shape without that assumption: the handler
writes its own bytes and returns `Result<(), anyhow::Error>`. ADR-0032 keeps
it as a secondary path for that reason: nothing else on the registration axis
accepts a signature with no serializable output and no render.

Reach for it when a command's job is genuinely "run this external process and
let it own the terminal" — streaming a subprocess's output live, driving an
interactive prompt library that writes ANSI itself, or wrapping a tool that
already produces its own formatted output — not for handlers that happen to
print instead of returning data.

## API

```rust
impl AppBuilder {
    pub fn command_passthrough<F>(self, path: &str, handler: F) -> Result<Self, SetupError>
    where
        F: FnMut(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext) -> Result<(), anyhow::Error> + 'static;
}
```

For a command declared inside `.commands(|g| ...)`, `GroupBuilder` has the
matching entry point:

```rust
impl GroupBuilder {
    pub fn passthrough<F>(self, name: &str, handler: F) -> Self
    where
        F: FnMut(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext) -> Result<(), anyhow::Error> + 'static;
}
```

Both take the same closure shape and register the command with no template:
there is nothing for a template to render.

## What it does not get

A passthrough command has no `Output` enum to return, so it gets none of the
things that come from having one:

- No template. The command is registered with its template reference set to
  "absent, silently" — there is no configured or conventional template to
  resolve, by design, not by omission.
- No render pass, so no theme, no style tags, no `Tabular` columns.
- No structured output modes. `Output::Render` is what `--output json` (and
  `yaml`/`xml`/`csv`) serializes; a passthrough handler never produces an
  `Output` value, so those modes have nothing to act on.
- No post-dispatch hooks. The passthrough dispatch closure is handed the
  command's `Hooks` and ignores them, so nothing runs between the handler
  returning and the empty result leaving dispatch.

App-level hooks registered for the command's path *do* still run, because they
sit outside the dispatch closure: a pre-dispatch hook runs before the handler
as it would for any command, and a post-output hook runs after it, receiving
`RenderedOutput::Silent`. A post-output hook attached to a passthrough command
is therefore not inert — it observes and can act, it just has no rendered text
to transform.

Concretely, under `--output json` (or any other output mode) a passthrough
command runs exactly the same as under the default: the dispatch closure
backing `command_passthrough`/`passthrough` takes the output mode as a
parameter and ignores it. Standout's own output-writing pipeline resolves the
command to an empty string every time — whatever the handler wrote, it wrote
directly (to stdout, stderr, a file, wherever), outside that pipeline, and
`--output` has no way to reach it.

## What the handler is responsible for

Because nothing downstream will format or emit anything on the handler's
behalf, the handler owns:

- Writing everything it wants seen — to stdout, stderr, or elsewhere.
- Its own error reporting for anything it prints before returning `Err(...)`;
  the `anyhow::Error` becomes the command's failure, but text already written
  stays written.
- Respecting (or explicitly ignoring) the user's terminal — colors, width,
  paging — since none of the framework's rendering machinery runs.

## Worked example

```rust
use anyhow::Context;
use clap::ArgMatches;
use standout::cli::{App, CommandContext};
use std::process::Command;

fn run_migrations(_matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> Result<(), anyhow::Error> {
    let status = Command::new("./migrate.sh")
        .status()
        .context("failed to launch migrate.sh")?;
    if !status.success() {
        anyhow::bail!("migrate.sh exited with {status}");
    }
    Ok(())
}

let app = App::builder()
    .command_passthrough("migrate", run_migrations)?
    .build()?;
```

`migrate.sh`'s own stdout and stderr reach the terminal unchanged; Standout
neither captures nor reformats them.

## When not to use it

The blessed path is a `#[handler]` function returning `Result<T, E>`, wrapped
in `Output::Render` and rendered through a template — see
[Handler Contract](../crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md). Reach for
that whenever the command has any data a caller might want as JSON, any
output a template could format, or any reason to support `--output`. Use
passthrough only when the handler's whole job is to hand control to
something else that already owns its own bytes.

32	- **I — Integrate with Clap.** Standout does not replace Clap. Clap remains the

38	  when a command needs configuration that is clearer in builder code.

43	pipeline in detail.

46	
47	- **I — Return data, not presentation.** A normal handler returns
48	  `Output::Render(data)`, `Output::Silent`, or `Output::Binary { ... }`. It
49	  should not print, emit ANSI, render a template, or branch on output mode.
50	- **I — Let the framework own the write for reported artifacts.** When a command
51	  produces a file *and* a report, return `Output::Artifact(...)` with owned bytes,
52	  an opt-in suggested destination, and the report. Standout selects the
53	  destination, writes, and renders the report afterwards with a receipt — the

76	  visible warning, not a substitute for validation.

78	  dispatch automatically flattens serializable data for CSV. The direct
79	  `render_auto_with_spec` API can render CSV with a `FlatDataSpec`, but arbitrary

81	  integrated. Prefer a stable CLI-owned view DTO, or record the missing app
82	  configuration seam.
83

85	[Templating](../crates/render/topics/templating.md),
86	[Styling System](../crates/render/topics/styling-system.md),

90

92

94	  persistence through the CLI-free Rust interface.
95	- **I — Adapter tests:** call the typed handler function directly and assert the
96	  CLI-to-core mapping plus returned view DTO.

1	# The Styling System
2	
3	`standout-render` uses a theme-based styling system where named styles are applied to content through bracket notation tags. Instead of embedding ANSI codes in your templates, you define semantic style names (`error`, `title`, `muted`) and let the theme decide the visual representation.
4	
5	This separation provides several benefits:
6	
7	- **Readability**: Templates use meaningful names, not escape codes
8	- **Maintainability**: Change colors in one place, update everywhere
9	- **Adaptability**: Themes can respond to light/dark mode automatically
10	- **Consistency**: Enforce visual hierarchy across your application
11	
12	---
13	
14	## Themes
15	
16	A `Theme` is a named collection of styles. Each style maps a name (like `title` or `error`) to visual attributes (bold cyan, dim red, etc.).
17	
18	### CSS Themes
19	
20	Define styles in standard CSS syntax — a subset of CSS Level 3 tailored for terminals:
21	
22	```css
23	/* theme.css */
24	.title {
25	    color: cyan;
26	    font-weight: bold;
27	}
28	
29	.error {
30	    color: red;
31	    font-weight: bold;
32	}
33	
34	.muted {
35	    opacity: 0.5;  /* maps to dim */
36	}
37	
38	.success {
39	    color: green;
40	}
41	
42	/* Shorthand works too */
43	.warning { color: yellow; }
44	```
45	
46	Load CSS themes:
47	
48	```rust
49	use standout_render::Theme;
50	
51	let theme = Theme::from_css(css_content)?;
52	```
53	
54	`Theme` parses a CSS string; reading the file is the caller's job:
55	
56	```rust
57	let css = std::fs::read_to_string("styles/theme.css")?;
58	let theme = Theme::from_css(&css)?;
59	```
60	
61	For a whole directory of themes with hot reload in debug builds, use
62	`AppBuilder::styles_dir` (see [App Configuration](../../../topics/app-configuration.md))
63	rather than reading a single file.
64	
65	CSS gives you syntax highlighting in editors, linting tools, and familiarity for web developers.
66	
67	### Programmatic Themes
68	
69	Build themes in code using the builder pattern:
70	
71	```rust
72	use standout_render::Theme;
73	use console::Style;
74	
75	let theme = Theme::new()
76	    .add("title", Style::new().bold().cyan())
77	    .add("error", Style::new().red().bold())
78	    .add("muted", Style::new().dim())
79	    .add("success", Style::new().green());
80	```
81	
82	> **Legacy format:** YAML themes are still supported via `Theme::from_yaml()`. CSS is the recommended format for all new projects.
83	
84	---
85	
86	## Supported Attributes
87	
88	### Colors
89	
90	| Attribute | CSS Property | Description             |
91	| --------- | ------------ | ----------------------- |
92	| `fg`      | `color`      | Foreground (text) color |
93	| `bg`      | `background` | Background color        |
94	
95	### Color Formats
96	
97	```css
98	/* Named colors (16 ANSI colors) */
99	.example { color: red; }
100	.example { color: green; }
101	.example { color: cyan; }
102	.example { color: magenta; }
103	.example { color: yellow; }
104	.example { color: white; }
105	.example { color: black; }
106	
107	/* Bright variants */
108	.example { color: bright_red; }
109	.example { color: bright_green; }
110	
111	/* 256-color palette (0-255) */
112	.example { color: 208; }
113	
114	/* RGB hex */
115	.example { color: #ff6b35; }
116	.example { color: #f63; }     /* shorthand */
117	
118	/* Theme-relative cube colors */
119	.example { color: cube(60%, 20%, 0%); }
120	```
121	
122	Cube colors express a position in a color cube whose 8 corners are the base ANSI
123	colors of the user's terminal theme. The same `cube(60%, 20%, 0%)` produces earthy
124	tones in Gruvbox, pastels in Catppuccin, and muted shades in Solarized.
125	Interpolation is done in CIE LAB space for perceptually uniform gradients.
126	Attach a palette to a theme with `Theme::with_palette()`.
127	
128	### Text Attributes
129	
130	| CSS Property                    | Effect            |
131	| ------------------------------- | ----------------- |
132	| `font-weight: bold`             | Bold text         |
133	| `opacity: 0.5`                  | Dimmed/faint text |
134	| `font-style: italic`            | Italic text       |
135	| `text-decoration: underline`    | Underlined text   |
136	| `text-decoration: blink`        | Blinking text     |
137	| `text-decoration: line-through` | Strikethrough     |
138	| `visibility: hidden`            | Hidden text       |
139	
140	---
141	
142	## Adaptive Styles (Light/Dark Mode)
143	
144	Terminal applications run in both light and dark environments. A color that looks great on a dark background may be illegible on a light one. `standout-render` solves this with adaptive styles.
145	
146	### How It Works
147	
148	Instead of defining separate "light theme" and "dark theme" files, you define mode-specific overrides at the style level:
149	
150	```css
151	.panel {
152	    font-weight: bold;
153	    color: gray;        /* Default/fallback */
154	}
155	
156	@media (prefers-color-scheme: light) {
157	    .panel { color: black; }   /* Override for light mode */
158	}
159	
160	@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
161	    .panel { color: white; }   /* Override for dark mode */
162	}
163	```
164	
165	When resolving `panel` in dark mode:
166	
167	1. Start with base attributes (`bold`, `gray`)
168	2. Merge dark overrides (`white` replaces `gray`)
169	3. Result: bold white text
170	
171	This is efficient: most styles (bold, italic, semantic colors like green/red) look fine in both modes. Only a handful need adjustment—typically foreground colors for contrast.
172	
173	### Programmatic API
174	
175	```rust
176	use standout_render::Theme;
177	use console::{Style, Color};
178	
179	let theme = Theme::new()
180	    .add_adaptive(
181	        "panel",
182	        Style::new().bold(),                     // Base (shared)
183	        Some(Style::new().fg(Color::Black)),     // Light mode
184	        Some(Style::new().fg(Color::White)),     // Dark mode
185	    );
186	```
187	
188	### Color Mode Detection
189	
190	`standout-render` auto-detects the OS color scheme when the caller probes the process:
191	
192	```rust
193	use standout_render::{ColorMode, TargetProperties};
194	
195	let properties = TargetProperties::detect();
196	match properties.color_scheme {
197	    ColorMode::Light => println!("Light mode"),
198	    ColorMode::Dark => println!("Dark mode"),
199	}
200	```
201	
202	`TargetProperties::detect()` is the one process probe, at the crate edge. Convenience wrappers call it then pass the result into `render_request`. Tests construct `TargetProperties` with an explicit `color_scheme` rather than installing a detector; `set_theme_detector` and the other detector override APIs are removed.
203	
204	---
205	
206	## Style Aliasing
207	
208	Aliases let semantic names resolve to visual styles. This is useful when multiple concepts share the same appearance:
209	
210	```rust
211	let theme = Theme::new()
212	    // Define the visual style once
213	    .add("title", Style::new().bold().cyan())
214	    // Aliases — pass a string to reference another style by name
215	    .add("commit-message", "title")
216	    .add("section-header", "title")
217	    .add("heading", "title");
218	```
219	
220	Now `[commit-message]`, `[section-header]`, and `[heading]` all render identically to `[title]`.
221	
222	Benefits:
223	
224	- Templates use meaningful, context-specific names
225	- Visual changes propagate automatically
226	- Refactoring visual design doesn't touch templates
227	
228	Aliases can chain: `a` → `b` → `c` → concrete style. Cycles are detected and rejected at load time.
229	
230	---
231	
232	## Unknown Style Tags
233	
234	When a template references a style not defined in the theme, `standout-render` handles it gracefully:
235	
236	| Output Mode | Behavior                                                   |
237	| ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
238	| `Term`      | Unknown tags get a `?` marker: `[unknown?]text[/unknown?]` |
239	| `Text`      | Tags stripped (plain text)                                 |
240	| `TermDebug` | Tags preserved as-is                                       |
241	
242	The `?` marker helps catch typos during development without crashing production apps.
243	
244	### Validation
245	
246	For strict checking at startup:
247	
248	```rust
249	use standout_render::validate_template;
250	
251	if let Err(error) = validate_template(template, &sample_data, &theme) {
252	    eprintln!("Unknown style tag: {}", error);
253	    std::process::exit(1);
254	}
255	```
256	
257	---
258	
259	## Built-in Styles
260	
261	`Theme::default()` includes adaptive styles for alternating table row backgrounds. These are used automatically when you pass `row_styles=true` (or a tint name) to the `table()` template function.
262	
263	| Style name              | Purpose                                 |
264	| ----------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
265	| `table_row_even`        | Even rows — no background (transparent) |
266	| `table_row_odd`         | Odd rows — subtle gray background shift |
267	| `table_row_even_gray`   | Alias for `table_row_even`              |
268	| `table_row_odd_gray`    | Alias for `table_row_odd`               |
269	| `table_row_even_blue`   | Even rows for blue tint                 |
270	| `table_row_odd_blue`    | Odd rows — dark navy / lavender bg      |
271	| `table_row_even_red`    | Even rows for red tint                  |
272	| `table_row_odd_red`     | Odd rows — dark crimson / blush bg      |
273	| `table_row_even_green`  | Even rows for green tint                |
274	| `table_row_odd_green`   | Odd rows — dark forest / mint bg        |
275	| `table_row_even_purple` | Even rows for purple tint               |
276	| `table_row_odd_purple`  | Odd rows — dark plum / lilac bg         |
277	
278	All odd-row styles are adaptive: they resolve to a dark variant when the terminal is in dark mode, and a light variant in light mode. You can override any of these by defining the same style name in your theme.
279	
280	---
281	
282	## Best Practices
283	
284	### Semantic, Presentation, and Visual Layers
285	
286	Organize your styles in three conceptual layers:
287	
288	**1. Visual primitives** (low-level appearance):
289	
290	```css
291	._cyan-bold { color: cyan; font-weight: bold; }
292	._dim { opacity: 0.5; }
293	._red-bold { color: red; font-weight: bold; }
294	```
295	
296	**2. Presentation roles** (UI concepts — use aliases in code):
297	
298	```rust
299	theme.add("heading", "_cyan-bold")
300	     .add("secondary", "_dim")
301	     .add("danger", "_red-bold");
302	```
303	
304	**3. Semantic names** (domain concepts — aliases to presentation):
305	
306	```rust
307	// In templates, use these
308	theme.add("task-title", "heading")
309	     .add("task-status-done", "success")
310	     .add("task-status-pending", "warning")
311	     .add("error-message", "danger");
312	```
313	
314	Templates use semantic names (`task-title`), which resolve to presentation roles (`heading`), which resolve to visual primitives (`_cyan-bold`).
315	
316	This layering lets you:
317	
318	- Refactor visuals without touching templates
319	- Maintain consistency across domains
320	- Document the purpose of each style
321	
322	### Naming Conventions
323	
324	```css
325	/* Good: descriptive, semantic */
326	.error-message { ... }
327	.file-path { ... }
328	.command-name { ... }
329	
330	/* Avoid: visual descriptions */
331	.red-text { ... }
332	.bold-cyan { ... }
333	```
334	
335	### Keep Themes Focused
336	
337	One theme per "look". Don't mix concerns:
338	
339	```text
340	styles/
341	├── default.css          # your app's default look
342	├── colorblind.css       # accessibility variant
343	└── monochrome.css       # for piped output
344	```
345	
346	---
347	
348	## API Reference
349	
350	### Theme Creation
351	
352	```rust
353	// From CSS string
354	let theme = Theme::from_css(css_str)?;
355	
356	// Empty theme (for programmatic building)
357	let theme = Theme::new();
358	
359	// Legacy: YAML is still supported
360	let theme = Theme::from_yaml(yaml_str)?;
361	```
362	
363	### Adding Styles
364	
365	```rust
366	// Static style
367	theme.add("name", Style::new().bold());
368	
369	// Adaptive style
370	theme.add_adaptive("name", base_style, light_override, dark_override);
371	
372	// Alias
373	theme.add("alias", "target_style");
374	```
375	
376	### Resolving Styles
377	
378	```rust
379	// Get the mode-agnostic style
380	let style: Option<Style> = theme.get_style("title", None);
381	
382	// Get style resolved for a specific mode
383	let style = theme.get_style("panel", Some(ColorMode::Dark));
384	```
385	
386	### Color Mode
387	
388	```rust
389	use standout_render::{ColorMode, TargetProperties};
390	
391	// Auto-detect at the crate edge
392	let properties = TargetProperties::detect();
393	let mode = properties.color_scheme;
394	
395	// Tests construct TargetProperties instead of installing a detector
396	let mut target = properties;
397	target.color_scheme = ColorMode::Light;
398	```
399

1	# Introduction to Dispatch
2	
3	CLI applications typically mix business logic with output formatting: database queries interleaved with `println!`, validation tangled with ANSI codes, error handling scattered across presentation. The result is code that's hard to test, hard to change, and impossible to reuse.
4	
5	`standout-dispatch` enforces a clean separation:
6	
7	```text
8	CLI args → Handler (adapter) → View data → consuming framework
9	```
10	
11	- **Handlers** receive parsed arguments, return serializable data
12	- **Hooks** intercept execution at defined points
13	
14	This isn't just architectural nicety—it unlocks:
15	
16	- **Testable handlers** — Typed adapters with explicit inputs and outputs
17	- **Reusable results** — JSON, templates, and plain text can all start from the same handler data
18	- **Cross-cutting concerns** — Auth, logging, transformation via hooks
19	- **Incremental adoption** — Migrate one command at a time
20	
21	---
22	
23	## The Problem
24	
25	Here's a typical CLI command implementation:
26	
27	```rust
28	fn list_command(matches: &ArgMatches) {
29	    let verbose = matches.get_flag("verbose");
30	    let items = storage::list().expect("failed to list");
31	
32	    println!("\x1b[1;36mItems\x1b[0m");
33	    println!("──────");
34	    for item in &items {
35	        if verbose {
36	            println!("{}: {} (created: {})", item.id, item.name, item.created);
37	        } else {
38	            println!("{}: {}", item.id, item.name);
39	        }
40	    }
41	    println!("\n{} items total", items.len());
42	}
43	```
44	
45	Problems with this approach:
46	
47	1. **Testing is painful** — You have to capture stdout and parse it
48	2. **No format flexibility** — Want JSON output? Write a whole new function
49	3. **Error handling is crude** — `expect` or scattered error messages
50	4. **Logic and presentation intertwined** — Can't reuse the logic elsewhere
51	5. **Cross-cutting concerns require duplication** — Auth checks in every command
52	
53	---
54	
55	## The Solution: Handlers Return Data
56	
57	With `standout-dispatch`, handlers adapt CLI input into application calls and
58	return view data:
59	
60	```rust
61	use standout_dispatch::{Handler, Output, CommandContext, HandlerResult};
62	use serde::Serialize;
63	
64	#[derive(Serialize)]
65	struct ListResult {
66	    items: Vec<Item>,
67	    total: usize,
68	}
69	
70	fn list_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<ListResult> {
71	    let items = storage::list()?;  // Errors propagate naturally
72	    Ok(Output::Render(ListResult {
73	        total: items.len(),
74	        items,
75	    }))
76	}
77	```
78	
79	The handler:
80	
81	- Receives parsed arguments (`&ArgMatches`) and execution context
82	- Returns a `Result` with serializable data
83	- Contains zero presentation logic
84	
85	Presentation is handled separately by the caller or by the `standout` framework.
86	
87	---
88	
89	## Quick Start
90	
91	```toml
92	[dependencies]
93	standout-dispatch = "9"
94	clap = { version = "4", features = ["derive"] }
95	serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
96	serde_json = "1"
97	anyhow = "1"
98	```
99	
100	```rust
101	use standout_dispatch::{
102	    FnHandler, Output, CommandContext, HandlerResult,
103	    extract_command_path, path_to_string,
104	};
105	use clap::{Command, Arg};
106	use serde::Serialize;
107	
108	#[derive(Serialize)]
109	struct Greeting { message: String }
110	
111	fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
112	    // 1. Define clap command
113	    let cmd = Command::new("myapp")
114	        .subcommand(
115	            Command::new("greet")
116	                .arg(Arg::new("name").required(true))
117	        );
118	
119	    // 2. Create handler
120	    let greet_handler = FnHandler::new(|matches, _ctx| {
121	        let name: &String = matches.get_one("name").unwrap();
122	        Ok(Output::Render(Greeting {
123	            message: format!("Hello, {}!", name),
124	        }))
125	    });
126	
127	    // 3. Parse and dispatch
128	    let matches = cmd.get_matches();
129	    let path = extract_command_path(&matches);
130	
131	    if path_to_string(&path) == "greet" {
132	        let ctx = CommandContext { command_path: path };
133	        let result = greet_handler.handle(&matches, &ctx)?;
134	
135	        if let Output::Render(data) = result {
136	            println!("{}", serde_json::to_string_pretty(&data)?);
137	        }
138	    }
139	
140	    Ok(())
141	}
142	```
143	
144	---
145	
146	## The Output Enum
147	
148	Handlers return one of three output types:
149	
150	```rust
151	pub enum Output<T: Serialize> {
152	    Render(T),          // Data for rendering
153	    Silent,             // No output (side-effect commands)
154	    Binary {            // Raw bytes (file exports)
155	        data: Vec<u8>,
156	        filename: String,
157	    },
158	}
159	```
160	
161	### Output::Render(T)
162	
163	The common case. Data is passed to your render function:
164	
165	```rust
166	fn list_handler(_m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Vec<Item>> {
167	    let items = storage::list()?;
168	    Ok(Output::Render(items))
169	}
170	```
171	
172	### Output::Silent
173	
174	For commands with side effects only:
175	
176	```rust
177	fn delete_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<()> {
178	    let id: &String = matches.get_one("id").unwrap();
179	    storage::delete(id)?;
180	    Ok(Output::Silent)
181	}
182	```
183	
184	### Output::Binary
185	
186	For generating files:
187	
188	```rust
189	fn export_handler(_m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<()> {
190	    let data = generate_report()?;
191	    let csv_bytes = format_as_csv(&data)?;
192	
193	    Ok(Output::Binary {
194	        data: csv_bytes.into_bytes(),
195	        filename: "report.csv".into(),
196	    })
197	}
198	```
199	
200	---
201	
202	## State Management
203	
204	Handlers access state through `CommandContext`, which provides two injection mechanisms:
205	
206	### App State (Shared)
207	
208	Configure long-lived resources at build time:
209	
210	```rust
211	use standout::cli::App;
212	
213	struct Database { /* connection pool */ }
214	struct Config { api_url: String }
215	
216	App::builder()
217	    .app_state(Database::connect()?)  // Shared across all dispatches
218	    .app_state(Config::load()?)
219	    .commands(|g| g.command_with("list", list_handler, |c| c.template_name("list")))?
220	    .build()?
221	```
222	
223	Access in handlers via `ctx.app_state`:
224	
225	```rust
226	fn list_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Vec<Item>> {
227	    let db = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Database>()?;
228	    let config = ctx.app_state.get_required::<Config>()?;
229	    Ok(Output::Render(db.list(&config.api_url)?))
230	}
231	```
232	
233	### Extensions (Per-Request)
234	
235	Pre-dispatch hooks inject request-scoped state via `ctx.extensions`:
236	
237	```rust
238	Hooks::new().pre_dispatch(|matches, ctx| {
239	    let user_id = matches.get_one::<String>("user").unwrap();
240	    ctx.extensions.insert(UserScope { user_id: user_id.clone() });
241	    Ok(())
242	})
243	```
244	
245	> For full details, see [App State and Extensions](../topics/app-state.md).
246	
247	---
248	
249	## Hooks: Cross-Cutting Concerns
250	
251	Hooks let you intercept execution without modifying handler logic:
252	
253	```rust
254	use standout_dispatch::{Hooks, HookError, RenderedOutput};
255	
256	let hooks = Hooks::new()
257	    // Before handler: validation, auth, inject per-request state
258	    .pre_dispatch(|matches, ctx| {
259	        if !is_authenticated() {
260	            return Err(HookError::pre_dispatch("auth required"));
261	        }
262	        Ok(())
263	    })
264	    // After handler, before render: transform data
265	    .post_dispatch(|_m, _ctx, mut data| {
266	        if let Some(obj) = data.as_object_mut() {
267	            obj.insert("timestamp".into(), json!(Utc::now().to_rfc3339()));
268	        }
269	        Ok(data)
270	    })
271	    // After render: transform output
272	    .post_output(|_m, _ctx, output| {
273	        if let RenderedOutput::Text(s) = output {
274	            Ok(RenderedOutput::Text(format!("{}\n-- footer", s)))
275	        } else {
276	            Ok(output)
277	        }
278	    });
279	```
280	
281	### Hook Phases
282	
283	| Phase | Timing | Receives | Can |
284	| ------- | -------- | ---------- | ----- |
285	| `pre_dispatch` | Before handler | ArgMatches, **&mut** Context | Abort execution, inject state |
286	| `post_dispatch` | After handler, before render | ArgMatches, Context, Data | Transform data |
287	| `post_output` | After render | ArgMatches, Context, Output | Transform output |
288	
289	> **State Injection:** Pre-dispatch hooks can inject dependencies via `ctx.extensions` that handlers retrieve. This enables dependency injection without changing handler signatures. See [App State and Extensions](../topics/app-state.md#extensions-per-request-state) for details.
290	
291	### Hook Chaining
292	
293	Multiple hooks per phase run sequentially:
294	
295	```rust
296	Hooks::new()
297	    .post_dispatch(add_metadata)      // Runs first
298	    .post_dispatch(filter_sensitive)  // Receives add_metadata's output
299	```
300	
301	---
302	
303	## Handler Types
304	
305	### Closure Handlers
306	
307	Most handlers are simple closures:
308	
309	```rust
310	let handler = FnHandler::new(|matches, ctx| {
311	    let name: &String = matches.get_one("name").unwrap();
312	    Ok(Output::Render(Data { name: name.clone() }))
313	});
314	```
315	
316	### Trait Implementations
317	
318	For handlers with internal state:
319	
320	```rust
321	struct DbHandler {
322	    pool: DatabasePool,
323	}
324	
325	impl Handler for DbHandler {
326	    type Output = Vec<Row>;
327	
328	    fn handle(&self, matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Vec<Row>> {
329	        let query: &String = matches.get_one("query").unwrap();
330	        let rows = self.pool.query(query)?;
331	        Ok(Output::Render(rows))
332	    }
333	}
334	```
335	
336	### Struct Handlers (With State)
337	
338	When handlers need internal state with `&mut self`:
339	
340	```rust
341	impl Handler for Cache {
342	    type Output = Data;
343	
344	    fn handle(&mut self, matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Data> {
345	        self.invalidate();  // &mut self works
346	        Ok(Output::Render(self.get()?))
347	    }
348	}
349	```
350	
351	See [Handler Contract](../topics/handler-contract.md) for full details.
352	
353	---
354	
355	## Command Routing Utilities
356	
357	Extract and navigate clap's `ArgMatches`:
358	
359	```rust
360	use standout_dispatch::{
361	    extract_command_path,
362	    get_deepest_matches,
363	    has_subcommand,
364	    path_to_string,
365	};
366	
367	// myapp db migrate --steps 5
368	let path = extract_command_path(&matches);  // ["db", "migrate"]
369	let path_str = path_to_string(&path);       // "db.migrate"
370	let deep = get_deepest_matches(&matches);   // ArgMatches for "migrate"
371	```
372	
373	---
374	
375	## Testing Handlers
376	
377	Because handlers have explicit inputs and outputs, testing their CLI adapter
378	behavior is straightforward:
379	
380	```rust
381	#[test]
382	fn test_list_handler() {
383	    let cmd = Command::new("test")
384	        .arg(Arg::new("verbose").long("verbose").action(ArgAction::SetTrue));
385	    let matches = cmd.try_get_matches_from(["test", "--verbose"]).unwrap();
386	
387	    let ctx = CommandContext {
388	        command_path: vec!["list".into()],
389	    };
390	
391	    let result = list_handler(&matches, &ctx);
392	
393	    assert!(result.is_ok());
394	    if let Ok(Output::Render(data)) = result {
395	        assert!(data.verbose);
396	    }
397	}
398	```
399	
400	No mocking needed—construct `ArgMatches` with clap, call your handler, assert on the result.
401	
402	---
403	
404	## Summary
405	
406	`standout-dispatch` provides:
407	
408	1. **Clean separation** — Handlers return data, renderers produce output
409	2. **Pluggable rendering** — Use any output format without changing handlers
410	3. **Hook system** — Cross-cutting concerns without code duplication
411	4. **Testable design** — CLI-free library behavior and typed handler adapters have explicit contracts
412	5. **Incremental adoption** — Migrate one command at a time
413	
414	For complete API details, see the [API documentation](https://docs.rs/standout-dispatch).
415	
416	> **For standout framework users:** The framework provides full integration with templates and themes. See the standout documentation for the `App` and `AppBuilder` APIs that wire dispatch and render together automatically.

input.content:
#! standout-answers 1
#! questionnaire: corpus.exit
#! fingerprint: sha256:64291870245510dad73ca960fd4024db9b9c161113a3dcc9c7e57a30973663fc

1. Summarize what you built and what state it is in. (text) <id:summary>

`ghlike` is complete: `cargo build` (debug and release) succeeds with no code
warnings, `cargo test` passes 18 unit tests, and I verified every example in
SPEC.md against the real binary at the byte level with `od -c`.

Layout in `app/src`:

- `forge.rs` — the frozen forge state. CLI-free: no clap, no standout, no
  wording of diagnostics. Lookups return `Option`.
- `view.rs` — CLI-owned view DTOs. Also resolves the padded-column widths,
  because the spec's layout rule ("each column but the last padded to its
  widest rendered cell, header included when shown") is content-driven; the
  templates pad with `pad_right(<width>)`. This is the split standout's own
  help rendering uses (`HelpData` carries `options_width`, the template carries
  the `pad_right` call).
- `machine.rs` — `--json <fields>`: parses the comma-separated field list,
  rejects unknown fields, and assembles the JSON bytes.
- `diagnostic.rs` — the three domain errors, each an exit-1 failure carrying its
  exact stderr text.
- `handlers.rs` — five adapters, grouped into `auth` / `repo` / `pr` /
  `pr_checks` submodules so `repo view` and `pr view` do not collide on the
  handler name `view`.
- `main.rs` — the clap tree, `#[derive(Dispatch)]` with `#[dispatch(nested)]`
  for the `auth` / `repo` / `pr` / `pr checks` groups, and `App` assembly.
- `templates/{auth/status,repo/view,pr/list,pr/view,pr/checks/list}.jinja` and
  `styles/default.css`.

Design decisions worth naming:

- The human surface renders through templates and is styled; the `--json`
  surface returns `Output::Render`'s sibling `Output::Binary`, which reaches
  stdout without a render pass. I confirmed with `--output=term` that the JSON
  bytes are identical when the destination reports colour support, which is
  what "never styled ... even on an attended color-capable terminal" asks for.
- I disabled standout's own `--output` and `--output-file-path` with
  `.no_output_flag()` / `.no_output_file_flag()`, so the flag surface is exactly
  SPEC.md's and any other flag is an unknown flag (exit 2).
- `<number>` is taken as a string, so `ghlike pr view abc` is the domain error
  `ghlike: no pull request found: abc` (exit 1) rather than a clap usage error.
  SPEC.md's exit-2 row enumerates "group without subcommand, unknown subcommand
  or flag", which does not cover a bad argument value, and the message echoes
  `<number>` verbatim.

Three things SPEC.md leaves open, where I picked and pinned a behaviour:

- JSON is compact (no pretty-printing) on a single line with one trailing
  newline — the same bytes a pipe and a terminal both see.
- Object keys come out in the order the caller requested them (`serde_json`
  with `preserve_order`), not sorted.
- The unknown-field message is `ghlike: unknown JSON field: "branch"` followed
  by `valid fields: number, title, state, author, draft`. SPEC.md only requires
  that it name the rejected field and list the valid ones.

2. Which of the provided documentation files (under docs/) did you actually consult? List their paths. (text) <id:sources.docs>

Read in full:

- docs/index.md
- docs/guides/tldr-intro-to-standout.md
- docs/guides/minimal-single-crate.md
- docs/guides/production-shaped-example.md
- docs/guides/leveraging-standout.md
- docs/topics/dispatch-attributes.md
- docs/topics/output-modes.md
- docs/topics/error-handling.md
- docs/topics/execution-outcomes.md
- docs/topics/app-configuration.md
- docs/topics/standout-help.md
- docs/topics/list-view.md
- docs/topics/passthrough.md
- docs/crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md
- docs/crates/dispatch/guides/intro-to-dispatch.md
- docs/crates/render/topics/templating.md
- docs/crates/render/topics/styling-system.md
- docs/crates/render/guides/intro-to-tabular.md

The ones that actually decided the implementation were dispatch-attributes.md
(nesting, registration paths, template-name convention, the `pure` return-type
constraint), handler-contract.md (the `Output` shapes), templating.md (the
trailing-newline contract and the filter list), execution-outcomes.md and
error-handling.md (streams and statuses), standout-help.md (the
width-in-data + `pad_right`-in-template idiom), and intro-to-tabular.md
(why `tabular()` could not resolve the widths for me).

Not consulted: the input, pipe, testing, topics-system, seeker, stability,
partial-adoption, app-state, template-engines, file-system-resources,
answer-sheets, upgrading-*, derived-questionnaires, bootstrap-a-project,
intro-to-standout, intro-to-testing, intro-to-rendering, and design docs.

3. Did you rely on anything beyond the provided docs/ — web search, prior knowledge of standout internals, other repositories or source code? Say exactly what, or answer 'none'. (text) <id:sources.external>

No web search, no standout source, no standout repository, no other
repositories. I did not open anything under the standout crates in the cargo
registry cache.

I did rely on two things outside docs/:

- **Prior knowledge of clap 4's derive macro**, which docs/ does not document
  and explicitly leaves to clap ("Standout does not replace Clap"). Specifically:
  that `#[derive(Subcommand)]` treats a single-field tuple variant as `Args` by
  default and needs `#[command(subcommand)]` **on the variant** to nest another
  `Subcommand` enum; that a non-`Option` subcommand field makes the subcommand
  required; and that clap's missing-subcommand and unknown-flag failures exit 2
  on stderr. docs/ shows the `Dispatch` side of nesting but never the clap side,
  so the doc's own snippet does not compile as written (see question 4).
- **General Rust/crates knowledge**: `serde_json`'s `preserve_order` feature for
  insertion-ordered object keys, and ordinary `serde`/`anyhow` usage.

Two smaller points, for completeness. `standout::cli::Extensions` does not exist
and docs/ never spells the import for it, so I found `standout_dispatch::Extensions`
by inference from the import block at the top of handler-contract.md's trait
section plus the compiler's `no Extensions in cli` error — from rustc's
diagnostics, not from reading the crate. And I used `--output=term` /
`--output=term-debug` as a temporary probe during development (I re-enabled the
flag, inspected the styled bytes, then disabled it again); that behaviour is
documented in output-modes.md.

4. Friction points, if any: for each, quote the exact command, error message, or doc passage that caused it. (text, optional) <id:friction>

**1. The `#[dispatch(nested)]` example does not compile against clap.**
dispatch-attributes.md says nested "Requires a single-field tuple variant
wrapping another `Dispatch` enum" and shows:

```rust
#[derive(Dispatch)]
#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
enum Commands {
    #[dispatch(nested)]
    Pr(PrCommands),
}
```

Writing that alongside `#[derive(Subcommand)]` — which the tldr guide and
minimal-single-crate both do — gives:

```
error[E0277]: the trait bound `PrCommands: clap::Args` is not satisfied
  --> src/main.rs:37:31
   |
37 |     Pr(#[command(subcommand)] PrCommands),
   |                               ^^^^^^^^^^ unsatisfied trait bound
   |
help: the trait `clap::Args` is not implemented for `PrCommands`
```

clap reads a single-field tuple variant as flattened `Args`. My first fix,
putting `#[command(subcommand)]` on the unnamed field, produced the same error;
it has to sit on the variant:

```rust
#[command(subcommand)]
#[dispatch(nested)]
Pr(PrCommands),
```

Nothing in docs/ pairs the two attributes, and the tuple-variant requirement is
precisely the shape clap needs an extra attribute for.

**2. Owning the exact stderr text of a domain error.** SPEC.md fixes the wording
(`ghlike: repository not found: <owner/name>`) and the status (1). error-handling.md
says an ordinary handler error is reframed:

> Standout formats the message as `Error: {error}` — the error's own `Display`
> text after that fixed prefix

so `?` on an `anyhow::Error` cannot produce it. The only documented escape is
`ExternalFailure`, which the same page scopes narrowly:

> Use `ExternalFailure` only when another operation owns the status and
> diagnostic contract, such as a delegated Git invocation.

`ghlike` delegates to nothing. I used it anyway — its contract ("The diagnostic
is a verbatim stderr payload: Standout adds no `Error:` prefix and no trailing
newline") is exactly what the spec needs — and isolated it in `diagnostic.rs`.
See question 6.

**3. Content-driven column widths.** SPEC.md: "each column but the last padded
to its widest rendered cell (header included when shown)". intro-to-tabular.md
rules `tabular()` out:

> A `{"min": ..., "max": ...}` column is resolved once, when `tabular()` or
> `table()` builds the formatter, before any row is seen — it does not measure
> row content. ... Resolving a top-level column's width from every row's content
> — the whole table, not just one row — is issue #359

and leveraging-standout.md reads as if it were covered: "Use tabular layout for
column relationships. ... do not hand-pad strings in handlers." I resolved the
widths in the view DTO and padded in the template with `pad_right`, which is the
idiom standout's own help rendering uses (standout-help.md: "There are no
`padding` fields. A row aligns itself by padding its name to its section's width
with `pad_right`"). It works, and the `--output=term-debug` dump confirms the
padding lands outside the style tags, but it took reading three pages to
conclude that the tabular system was the wrong tool here.

**4. Emitting n rows with n-1 newlines.** templating.md's trailing-newline
contract is clear and correct ("The engine consumes exactly one final newline",
"`App::run` writes ... with `writeln!`"), but it means a loop template must
render *without* a trailing newline. For `pr list` the header line anchors it
and `{%- for %}` / `{%- endfor %}` is clean. The headerless `pr checks list` has
no anchor, so every straightforward arrangement is off by one newline at one end
or the other, and I ended up with:

```jinja
{% for check in checks %}{% if not loop.first %}
{% endif %}{{ ... }}{% endfor %}
```

A worked example of a bare repeating block would have saved the byte-level
trial and error.

5. Places the documentation was wrong or missing, if any: quote what the doc says and what actually happened. (text, optional) <id:docs.gaps>

**1. `CommandContext`'s `app_state` is described two ways on one page.**
handler-contract.md's struct listing says:

```rust
pub struct CommandContext {
    pub command_path: Vec<String>,
    pub app_state: Rc<Extensions>,
    pub extensions: Extensions,
}
```

and eleven lines later, about the same field:

> **app_state**: Shared, immutable state configured at app build time via
> `AppBuilder::app_state()`. Wrapped in `Arc` for cheap cloning.

Its own test example then writes `app_state: Arc::new(app_state)`, while
tldr-intro-to-standout.md shows `Rc<Extensions>`. I sidestepped it with
`app_state: app_state.into()`, which compiles either way.

**2. `Extensions` has no documented import path, and the obvious one is wrong.**
handler-contract.md's "Testing with App State" example calls `Extensions::new()`
with no `use` line for it. `use standout::cli::Extensions;` fails:

```
error[E0432]: unresolved import `standout::cli::Extensions`
  --> src/handlers.rs:122:9
   |
122 |     use standout_dispatch::Extensions;
   |         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ no `Extensions` in `cli`
```

`standout_dispatch::Extensions` is the path. Every other type in that example
(`CommandContext`, `Output`, `Handler`) *is* re-exported under `standout::cli`,
so the one that isn't is the one worth spelling out.

**3. intro-to-dispatch.md is stale in two places.** It presents the `Output`
enum as three variants:

> ```rust
> pub enum Output<T: Serialize> {
>     Render(T),          // Data for rendering
>     Silent,             // No output (side-effect commands)
>     Binary { ... },
> }
> ```

with no `Artifact` and no `#[non_exhaustive]`, both of which handler-contract.md
documents. Its quick-start also builds `CommandContext { command_path: path }`,
which cannot compile against the three-field struct. Neither cost me anything,
because handler-contract.md is right, but a reader who starts at the crate
intro gets a shape that does not exist.

**4. Nothing documents how to keep an application's own machine-output flag
unrendered.** output-modes.md is emphatic that mode selection is the framework's
(`--output`) and that a handler must not branch on it: "Output mode is a
rendering concern and is deliberately absent from `CommandContext`." A CLI in
the gh mold has its own `--json <fields>` with field selection, which no
`--output` value can express — the field list changes the *shape* of the
document, not just its format. `Output::Binary` is the shape that does it, but
output-modes.md, handler-contract.md and intro-to-dispatch.md all describe
Binary purely as file export ("Raw bytes for file output", "For generating
files", `report.pdf` / `report.csv` examples). Only leveraging-standout.md's
one-line invariant — "A normal handler returns `Output::Render(data)`,
`Output::Silent`, or `Output::Binary { ... }`" — hints that it is a general
normal-output shape. Nothing says outright what execution-outcomes.md's table
implies and what I confirmed empirically: with no `--output-file-path`, Binary
bytes go to stdout verbatim, no theme, no template, no trailing newline added.

**5. Two behaviours I had to determine by running the binary, both undocumented
and both fine.** An `Output::Render` whose template renders to the empty string
(`ghlike pr checks list 3`, a pull request with no checks) writes *nothing* to
stdout — not the bare `\n` that templating.md's "`App::run` writes ... with
`writeln!`" would predict. And `Output::Binary` bytes are written with no
newline appended, so a JSON emitter must supply its own.

6. Workarounds you left in the produced code, if any. (text, optional) <id:workarounds>

**1. `ExternalFailure` for domain errors that delegate to nothing.**
`app/src/diagnostic.rs` wraps all three exit-1 diagnostics
(`ghlike: repository not found: …`, `ghlike: no pull request found: …`,
`ghlike: unknown JSON field: …`) in `ExternalFailure::new(1, …)` so the stderr
payload stays verbatim and the status stays exactly 1. error-handling.md scopes
that type to preserving another executable's contract; there is no other
executable here. It is the only documented way to own an error's exact stderr
wording, so I used it, confined it to one module, and said why in that module's
doc comment. The framework gap is: no documented seam for an application-owned
diagnostic that is not a delegated process.

**2. `Output::Binary` as the `--json` channel.** `app/src/handlers.rs` returns
`Output::Binary { data, filename }` for `--json`, with `filename` set to a name
nothing ever uses — `--output-file-path` is disabled, so the framework always
writes the bytes to stdout and never touches a file. handler-contract.md is
explicit that this is safe ("The filename is a **hint for the caller**, not
permission to write. Without `--output-file-path`, `run()` sends the bytes to
stdout and touches no file"), but carrying a dead filename to get
"bytes straight to stdout" is a workaround for the absence of a shape that says
exactly that.

**3. Character counting for column widths.** `app/src/view.rs::width` counts
`chars()` rather than terminal columns. The frozen forge state is ASCII, so the
two agree; standout exposes `display_width` as a MiniJinja filter but docs/
names no Rust-side equivalent I could call from the view. The templates' own
`pad_right` does measure display width, so only the width *resolution* has this
limit, and a non-ASCII title is the only thing that would expose it.

**4. `{% if not loop.first %}` for the headerless table.**
`app/src/templates/pr/checks/list.jinja` emits its row separators with a
`loop.first` test rather than plain newlines, to satisfy the trailing-newline
contract described in question 4. Correct, but it reads worse than the
`{%- for %}` form the header-bearing `pr/list.jinja` gets to use.

7. How confident are you that the acceptance criteria in SPEC.md pass? (low, medium, or high) <id:confidence>

high

Layout in `app/src`:

- `forge.rs` — the frozen forge state. CLI-free: no clap, no standout, no
  wording of diagnostics. Lookups return `Option`.
- `view.rs` — CLI-owned view DTOs. Also resolves the padded-column widths,
  because the spec's layout rule ("each column but the last padded to its
  widest rendered cell, header included when shown") is content-driven; the
  templates pad with `pad_right(<width>)`. This is the split standout's own
  help rendering uses (`HelpData` carries `options_width`, the template carries
  the `pad_right` call).
- `machine.rs` — `--json <fields>`: parses the comma-separated field list,
  rejects unknown fields, and assembles the JSON bytes.
- `diagnostic.rs` — the three domain errors, each an exit-1 failure carrying its
  exact stderr text.
- `handlers.rs` — five adapters, grouped into `auth` / `repo` / `pr` /
  `pr_checks` submodules so `repo view` and `pr view` do not collide on the
  handler name `view`.
- `main.rs` — the clap tree, `#[derive(Dispatch)]` with `#[dispatch(nested)]`
  for the `auth` / `repo` / `pr` / `pr checks` groups, and `App` assembly.
- `templates/{auth/status,repo/view,pr/list,pr/view,pr/checks/list}.jinja` and
  `styles/default.css`.

- The human surface renders through templates and is styled; the `--json`
  surface returns `Output::Render`'s sibling `Output::Binary`, which reaches
  stdout without a render pass. I confirmed with `--output=term` that the JSON
  bytes are identical when the destination reports colour support, which is
  what "never styled ... even on an attended color-capable terminal" asks for.

  `.no_output_flag()` / `.no_output_file_flag()`, so the flag surface is exactly
  SPEC.md's and any other flag is an unknown flag (exit 2).
- `<number>` is taken as a string, so `ghlike pr view abc` is the domain error
  `ghlike: no pull request found: abc` (exit 1) rather than a clap usage error.

  or flag", which does not cover a bad argument value, and the message echoes
  `<number>` verbatim.

- JSON is compact (no pretty-printing) on a single line with one trailing
  newline — the same bytes a pipe and a terminal both see.

repositories. I did not open anything under the standout crates in the cargo
registry cache.

  and explicitly leaves to clap ("Standout does not replace Clap"). Specifically:

  default and needs `#[command(subcommand)]` **on the variant** to nest another

  required; and that clap's missing-subcommand and unknown-flag failures exit 2
  on stderr. docs/ shows the `Dispatch` side of nesting but never the clap side,
  so the doc's own snippet does not compile as written (see question 4).
